speechtext:
Last Friday the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Maedonnell) addressed the following question to me:
The daily press carries a report that Albert Edward De Palma has forfeited bail totalling $50,000 in the United States courts, which I presume was paid in United States funds. Can the minister tell us whether this money was obtained through the foreign exchange control board?
I have made inquiries and I find that the circumstances in this case, so far as the foreign exchange control board was concerned, are as follows:
Following De Palma's arrest in the United States, United States Fidelity and Guaranty Company, Toronto, which is a branch of an American company of the same name, advised us that De Palma had applied to the American company in the United States for a bail bond for $50,000. As collateral security for the bail bond, the American company was prepared to accept $62,500 in Canadian funds to be deposited with its Canadian branch. The board agreed to this arrangement on condition that in the event of a claim against United States Fidelity and Guaranty Company under the bail bond, there would be no commitment on the part of the board to approve a transfer of the collateral security which might be forfeited by the Canadian branch to the head office of the company in the United States.
As De Palma has now evidently forfeited his bail, the position would appear to be that United States Fidelity and Guaranty Company will forfeit the Canadian dollar collateral which will become part of the assets of the Canadian branch. The amount may not be transferred to the parent company in the United States in United States dollars or otherwise without the board's permission and in accordance with the condition notified to the company, it is not intended to authorize any such transfer.

I need not emphasize the value of the educational work which the many thousands of volunteer workers did through their own organizations and in their own communities, during the war and immediately following. It contributed in very large measure to the success of emergency programs conducted during this period.
It is these groups, desirous of carrying on work similar in nature to that which they found to be effective in the years of war emergency, who are now forming the representative body known as the Canadian association of consumers. The expenditure approved on their behalf was to assist in meeting initial expenses of organization only; they will conduct the affairs of the association on an entirely independent basis, through an annual membership fee.
It should be noted that as no sum was provided in the form of a grant, expenditures on behalf of the association have been made through the comptroller of the treasury, on the saftie basis as any other government expenditure.	[DOT]

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, February 2, consideration ' of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King that a select committee be appointed to examine and report on the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living and matters pertaining thereto, and -the amendment of Mr. Bracken.
Prices Committee

Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre)'. Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the house to consider the problem now before us not so much in terms of parliamentary procedure or in terms of unreal percentages, but rather as it actually confronts the vast majority of our Canadian people. I am sure those of us who have been brought into contact with people over the last number of years will realize the truth of my statement when I say that seldom have the Canadian people been so much upset, so much disturbed, so fearful of the future as they are at the present time. There is, indeed, almost a state of panic among many of our Canadian people as they find themselves face to face with the impossibility of making both ends meet. In addition to the fears of world insecurity that are round about us, and all the rest of it, this problem of high prices is really bearing heavily upon our people.
There is no point in hon. members opposite rising and saying a statement like this is running down Canada. Our concern here is not to compare conditions in Canada with the conditions that may exist in some less fortunate part of the world. Our concern is to face frankly the problems that confront our own people.
There may be a few people who are not greatly disturbed by the increase in the cost of living. Those whose incomes are S3,000, $4,000, or $5,000 a year or more can make adjustments' in their budgets to meet the increased costs of necessities. These higher prices mean for people in those brackets simply that they have to do without a few luxuries or save a little bit less; but they are not under any compulsion to do without necessities. The number of people who can make those adjustments is very limited. The great masses of our people, faced with rising prices, have to cut down on their consumption of milk, bread, butter and meat. In many cases they have discontinued altogether the use of orange juice and fresh fruits and vegetables; and in many instances it means denying their children cod liver oil and those other vitamin products which are necessary for the building of good health.
As one of the veterans organizations has put it, the problem has become one of actually keeping alive on the incomes people now have, in the light of today's high prices. I have mentioned veterans organizations, and that leads me to call attention in particular to the plight of veterans under present disability benefits, and to the plight that will still be theirs when those benefits have been increased by the amount announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). There

is also the serious plight of burnt-out pensioners and widows of non-pensioned veterans. There is the extreme difficulty many superannuated civil servants are facing, as well as the difficulties facing our old age pensioners and Canadians generally in the simple attempt to keep alive and to observe health and decent living standards, in the face of the wide gap existing today between the incomes of our people and the cost of living at a reasonable level.
I would urge upon members of the house the realization that the wide gap between the incomes of our people and the cost of living is not a matter of imagination in the minds of our people. If is borne out by government statistics. I shall have something to say in a few minutes about what I shall term the uselessness of the cost of living index still being used. However, before I come to those remarks about the cost of living index I am going to use that index, because poor criterion that it is, it tells at least part of the story.
The cost of living index, may I point out, merely gives us unreal percentages. It begins with a selected group of families, back in the years 1935 to 1939. As a matter of fact it deals with only some 1,400 or 1,500 Canadian families. It took families with incomes varying from $600 up to about $2,800, and struck an average. The bureau of statistics found at that time what a family with $1,453.80 was doing with its money. In other words, it found what that one family with that much income was spending its money on, and accepted that expenditure as normal, in other words. 100.
It was not normal for two reasons. On the one hand the amount of $1,453.80 was higher than the average wage level in that period, and also it was a mistaken figure, because even that amount was not sufficient to buy the necessities of life at that time.
The cost of living index, I repeat, is based on what an average family with $1,453.80 spent its money on in the period 1935-39. When we are told today that the cost of living index is 145 or 150 all it means is that it would cost today 145 per cent or 150 per cent of what it cost in 1935-39 to buy those particular commodities.
The commodities which were bought at that figure in 1939 included the following:
Food	 $ 443.00
Shelter	 260.50
Fuel and light	 90.50
Clothing	 165.80
Home furnishings	 125.70
Miscellaneous (health, personal care, transportation, recreation, life insurance)	 310.40
Other items	 39.90

Prices Committee
That amount of $1,453.80, which was the arbitrary base for the cost of living index in 1935-39, meant that that average person had to have an average weekly wage of $27.95 in order to buy the goods and services I have indicated. That, however, was not the average weekly wage in that period; according to the Labour Gazette it was about S2 a week less than that. But even taking that figure of $27.95 a week in the period 1935-39, I ask hon. members to consider what has happened. I now take the cost of living index on October 1, 1947, because that is the latest date for which there was a comparable figure in wage rates. The index for that date was placed at 142-2. This means that as at- October 1, 1947, in order to buy the selected list of necessities which were bought in 1935-39 for SI.453.80 it was necessary to have $2,067.30. In- other words what the cost of living index tells us is merely this, that in order to purchase the same quantity of goods and services that was chosen for that arbitrary family in 1935-39 it is now necessary to have $39.75 per week. But, according to the December 1947 issue of the Labour Gazette, page 1827, the average weekly earnings of wage earners in Canada today is only $37.37. or $2.38 a week short.

It does not include family allowances, but I shall come to that in a minute. May I point out that to agree to $2.38 a week as the actual shortage, one would have to assume that S2.057.30 is enough to maintain a decent standard of living today. Well, I have taken- the breakdown the dominion bureau of statistics took when- it built up this cost of living index. I have taken that breakdown- and increased the amount spent in 1935-39 on these various items by the percentage which each of those items have increased in price. That means that with $2,067.30, a family, in order to keep within the terms of the cost of living index, has to get along with food to a value of $758.86 a year or $14.59 a week. I submit that not a housewife in the country would admit that you can feed a Canadian family today on $14.59 a week. Those who have to do it simply have to get along without some of the important protective foods which are necessary in this country. That basis implies that one can get along today, so far as rent, is concerned, on $323.13, or $26.92 a month. That, too, everyone knows to be hopelessly inadequate even with the controls which have been maintained on residential rents. Fuel and light today would cost only SI 10.43 a year; the cost of these items is much higher. Clothing would work
out at $255.60 a year or $21.30 a month-again a figure that is altogether too low. Home furnishings would be S1SS.42 a year. How far can a family go today in- purchasing home furnishings with $188.42 to spend in a year? Then miscellaneous and other items add up to about $400 a year. I submit that that is inadequate when you realize that it has to cover health, personal care, transportation, life insurance and anything else which has not been named in the items I have given already.
Let us not put these things in percentages or unreal terms, let us look at them in dollars and cents and realize what the Canadian family really needs today. On my own responsibility I suggest these figures as a minimum of what a Canadian family should have. First, SIS per week for food. I base that upon the report made by the Toronto welfare council which was included in a book on nutrition and the production and distribution of food put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare and which I have adjusted according to the increases in the cost of food which have taken place since that budget was published in 1944.
Rent should be at least $8 per week or about $35 per month. Fuel and -light would have to be $4 per week and clothing, $6 per week. For an average family $6 per week would be just a gesture toward home furnishing. Then S10 per week would be needed for other things, health, transportation, recreation, and so on. Those minimum figures add up to $52 per week which would be required to provide a decent living at the present time. However, according to the Labour Gazette of December, 1947, page 1827, the average income of wage earners in Canada is $37.37 per week, which is $14.63 short of a minimum budget for a decent living at the present time.
A moment ago the hon. member for Stan-stead (Mr. Hackett) asked if -the figures I gave included family allowances. They did not; they were just the wages earned by those in that group. I would point out two things to him and to hon. members opposite. First of all, the purpose of family allowances was not to take up the slack.

Statistics should also be given as to how many families are in receipt of income sufficient to provide a decent standard of living; how many families are in receipt of income above that and how many are in receipt of income below that, and then separate those both above and below into various brackets.
Comparisons have been made from time to time between this country and other countries but I submit that it is difficult to arrive at anything definite because different bases are taken in different countries for their cost of living indices. speechtext:
Before anyone interjects that to put that much money into circulation would be inflationary, may I say, yes it would, and in order to prevent such inflationary effects price control must be put into effect as well, which is the policy we are advocating. It might even require a certain amount of rationing. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is no time for fooling around with useless committees of inquiry. This is no time for saying we cannot take this step because it does not fall in line with the policy of the party in power. We are facing a crisis in Canadian home life, in Canadian health, and in Canadian living standards, and it is time something was done about it by the government of the day.
One argument it is certainly no longer necessary to answer, and that is the point about the constitutionality of price controls and subsidies. Although the government was advancing that argument last year it is actually bringing in a bill now to extend controls for another year. So the power is to be there if the house grants it. But what the people of Canada are concerned about is whether those powers are to be used. The Prime Ministei made a great play yesterday on his opinion that the people of Canada want this committee. The people of Canada do not want another time-wasting committee, any more than the Prime Minister did in the days when he was objecting to committees. They want price controls and subsidies. They want the cost of living brought down or their incomes brought up. They want the government to make it possible for both ends to meet. I submit that if the Prime Minister has any doubt about it he should respond _ to the challenge given by the leader of this group yesterday and, if he is not prepared to go to the country, at least he should call by-elections in the three federal ridings that are now vacant.
Lest my time be exhausted before I do something I wish to attend to while on my feet, may I refer briefly to the amendment moved yesterday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). There is much in that amendment that is acceptable to us, particularly in the sense that it seeks to broaden the terms of reference. We like in particular the provision to give the power to the committee to make recommendations. But there are two points in the amendment that we simply could not accept in the form in which they were presented to the house. I refer to the clause having to do with the restoration of subsidies. So far as that clause is concerned we feel that it should be more specific, that it should ask for the restoration of both price controls and

subsidies, and direct the committee to examine this question immediately and make an early report to the house.
We also feel that the clause in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition regarding the situation in which our farmers find themselves is ambiguous and should be made clear. Therefore I propose to move an amendment which accepts the general structure of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition but changes the two clauses to which I have referred.
I therefore move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), that the amendment be amended by deleting paragraphs (e) and (f) of clause 1 thereof and substituting the following therefor-the clauses I shall now read will take the place of (e) and (f) in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, and it will come under the general heading asking the committee to examine and report on the following:
(e)	measures to stem the rising cost of living, such as the restoration of price controls and subsidies, the examination of these matters to be the committee's first order of business and a report thereon to be presented to this house not later than three weeks from the day of the committee's first meeting;
(f)	measures to control the prices of commodities entering into the farmers' costs of production in view of the fact that controls are maintained on the prices of farm products.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that (e) and (f) in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition need to be altered along the lines I have proposed and in particular that my clause (e) represents the feeling of the people of Canada at the present time. They do not want a committee at all. They want price controls and subsidies. But if the government is going to insist on the committee being set up, the people of Canada want that committee to consider first of all ways and means of stemming the rising cost of living, by such methods as price controls and subsidies, and not to take six months or a year to deal with the matter-the Stevens committee and commission took a full year-but to report immediately so that something may be done to avoid further suffering on the part of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry but
I was not able to be in the house yesterday afternoon to listen to the speech delivered by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken) or the speeches delivered by the leaders of the other groups. As a matter of fact I was elsewhere in the building dealing

Prices Committee
with some matters which were at the same time under discussion in the house. And, of course, since the committee which I was meeting with was not a committee of the house the discussions with regard to similar matters were going on here at the time we were attempting to deal with some of them elsewhere. I have, however, had the privilege of reading the addresses which were delivered yesterday afternoon, and it is my intention to spend most of the time available to me this afternoon in dealing with the address of the leader of the opposition. I do that because about three-quarters of his speech was taken up with agricultural matters, and in a manner in which they have been covered before, not only by the leader of the opposition but by other speakers in the house.
I shall not attempt therefore to follow too closely the statements made, or to answer them in particular, but will deal rather with the criticisms as related to the proposal now before the house.
It is suggested that a committee of this house composed of sixteen members be set up to act as a fact-finding body to 'place not only before this house but before the country all the facts available with regard to the present situation in Canada in relation to the cost of living. It is taken 'for granted by the government and by this side of the house that after we have that full information, either the house or the government, or the house and the government acting in cooperation, will be able to take such action as may be necessary, based upon that information.
In one part of his speech the leader of the opposition took the position that the government should take responsibility for policy. But in most of what he said and in what is contained in the latter part of the amendment which he moved he suggested that the government should place that responsibility upon the committee. The government has stated through different speakers from this side that we are prepared to take responsibility not only for what has been done by the government, or what is being done now, but for the necessary policy to be applied in the future in order to deal with this particular question.
In dealing with this matter, however, the leader of the opposition covered quite fully the subjects which he has discussed on many occasions since becoming leader of the Progressive Conservative party. I hold in my hand an advertisement which appeared in the Family Herald and Weekly Star of May 5849-51
9, 1945, the 'heading of which is, "A Farmer Fights for Farmers' Rights." It goes on to
state:
"I may say quite frankly that if it had not been for that part of your platform which provides for a square deal being given to agriculture, I would not have been here." (John Bracken . . .)
These are the words of the present leader of the official opposition. Then he goes on to outline what the platform is and what the intentions of the government would be if he were at the head of the government. The advertisement reads:
At last a farmer-fighting champion of the rights of farmers-strides into the political arena of this great dominion and demands as their God-given right, fair play for Canadian farmers, here and now.
And in order to obtain that fair play for Canadian farmers the advertisement goes on to say:
(1)	The farmers shall be guaranteed a proportionate share of the nation's income.
(2)	A permanent policy of forward contract prices shall be guaranteed to farmers by law.
(3)	The prices guaranteed will be calculated by a non-political council, and will be based on the farmers' proportionate share of the national income. These prices will be announced before the production seasons begin.
(4)	This policy would increase present average farm income by not less than twenty per cent.
We are setting out to remove the fear of a post-war collapse of agricultural income, such as occurred two years after the last war-
And may I pause to say, under a Conservative government.
-and such as manifested itself so disastrously in the ten years preceding this war.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that was the policy laid down on May 9, 1945, in an advertisement placed in one of the great farm periodicals of this country, and spread broadcast among the farmers of Canada. I should just like to say at this point that the speech delivered yesterday was largely an attempt to condemn the principles stated in that declaration of policy. Immediately following the appearance of that advertisement in the press, I as Minister of Agriculture stated to the people of Canada that everything essential to their welfare which was contained in the platform was already contained ini the policies being put into effect by the present government. Let me recall one or two of the sections I have just read in order to bring that back to mind: "A permanent policy of forward contract prices shall be guaranteed to farmers." Now, of course, he puts in, in big black letters, "by law". Well, there is no difference between the proposal made there and the policy which
Prices Committee

the leader of the opposition spent most of his speech yesterday condemning. He began by setting forth to the house that there is something wrong with the position of agriculture in Canada, and in order to emphasize that he was attempting to state to the house that the rising cost of living was largely due to increased costs of food. He said food products have most to do with the cause of criticism of the rising costs of living in Canada, and stated that whereas the cost of living had increased by only 46 points as compared with 1936-39, taking 1936-39 as 100, the cost of food products had increased by 78-7 per cent. That is in accordance with the statistics which were quoted to the house. From that time on, 'Mr. Speaker, he divided his time between trying to show that the cost of food is too high and trying to show that the cost of producing food is too high. When he found himself in difficulties with the farmers through trying to talk down their price level, he then spent a few paragraphs ini trying to convince his hearers that he should be saying something in criticism of the other members of the citizenship of this country, by criticizing the fact that their costs had gone up. But after he had spent considerable time in trying to prove to the house those two different propositions, he stated that the real cause of all this difficulty is the British contracts, which have attempted to freeze prices, and the embargo against the exportation of food products from Canada to the United States.
In the platform as laid down in 1945 there were to be contracts and those contracts were to establish prices for farmers. I should like to ask the leader of the opposition or any other member of this house the following question. With whom would those contracts be made if not with the one country in the world where there is a market for the surplus farm products of Canada 7 How' could they have been different, in principle at least, from the contracts which we now have with the British? Even if that had not been in the platform of the leader of the opposition, I would be inclined to ask this question, Mr. Speaker. If those contracts are bad, and if they have had the effect stated for them by the leader of the opposition, why is it that every farm organization in Canada, with one possible exception, is continually passing resolutions saying that they want the contracts and that they want them continued; that they want the stability, which is the basis of these contracts, continued; and in season and out are asking us to carry on under these contracts?
I have here on my desk statements coming recently from some of the organizations which
[Mr. Gardiner.!
deal with that particular matter. Something is said in criticism of the price which we have been receiving for poultry products, and I have here a letter from the secretary-treasurer of the Canadian poultry council, dated January 18, 1948, addressed to Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa, Ontario, and reading as follows:
Dear Sir:
During the recent conference of the directors of the National (now Canadian) Poultry Council held in Ottawa, January 13, 14, and 15, 1948, the matter of the recently negotiated contract for eggs with the British Ministry of Food was discussed at length.
It was the unanimous opinion of the directors of the council (representing each province) that the ultimate announcement made by you on January 2, 1948, was very satisfactory to the poultry industry of Canada at this time, as it helped to regain the confidence of the producers at the beginning of the crop year.
I was instructed, sir, to convey to you their appreciation on behalf of the industry they represent, realizing in small part the great difficult^ which you undoubtedly encountered.
That is -the opinion of some of the producer-who are presumed to be so greatly dissatisfied with the activities of the government in relation to these matters.

I went on to say that throughout the period of the war, and particularly during the last three or four years of the war, we in Canada had been intent on putting into effect in this country a policy which would stop the sort of rise in the cost of living that was discussed at great length yesterday by the leader of the opposition; that in order to halt this rising spiral of prices of the necessities of life we put controls on the prices of products and more particularly on the prices of foods, and that those price levels were held during the whole war. I went on to say that price levels are still higher in the United States than in Canada. To substantiate that statement I have the remarks made yesterday by the leader of the opposition, who said that industrial wages in Canada are only 70-3 per cent of those in the United States, and then went on to say that the cost of living in Canada is 77-7 per cent of the cost of living in the United States. In other words we have a lower cost of living in Canada as a result of our activities during and since the war.
Then I went on to say that our objective in that policy was the same both during the war and since. During the war the objective was to keep down the cost of production of those things needed for war and for carrying on activities in our own country, as far as it was possible to keep them down under the circumstances. Since the war we have had the same objective in mind, namely to keep down the cost of production in this country. And I say to farmers and industry alike that whether we like it or not, the Conservative policy of high costs, which has been associated with all their programs throughout the periods they have formed a government in Canada, has always proved detrimental to the development of industry and agriculture in this country. It does not make any difference whether or not you call it Conservative; throughout the ages that policy has been detrimental to the best interests of any country which attempted to build up industry within its bounds. Great Britain, which set an example to the world during the last half of the nineteenth century in the matter of industrial development, built that industry upon low costs of production. Their own people enjoyed a higher standard of living than the people of any other industrial country in the world, but low costs of production made it
Prices Committee

possible for them to sell their products to every nation in the world. As far as Canada is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we will only get back into the markets of the world and maintain our position there, when the nations come back to normal, by having our costs at reasonably low levels. Only thus may we sell our products to advantage in every part of the world.
So what I said to the people in Lethbridge was that for the time being it would take away most of the benefits we have obtained from the policies followed during the war if we were to immediately jump up to the United States price level. Someone said, "We are not asking you to do that." I replied: Well, you are asking the opportunity to sell our beef in the United States; and they said that was right. I went on to say that our experience up to the present has been that none of our high priced beef goes outside Canada; that with the purchasing power we have in this country today the Canadian people are going to eat their own. high quality beef. And I went on to point out that if the Canadian people should bid the United States price or more in order to keep that beef in this country, that would not bring United States dollars into Canada but would bring about a higher price level in this country, because if you had it for beef you would require to have it for every other agricultural product. So this resolution was passed at that conference the next day and sent down to Winnipeg. There the national organization passed it with the provision I read to the house, namely that it should be an objective of government policy. And that is the objective of government policy, to put our beef back on the United States market, at a time when the price levels of the two countries make this possible without upsetting the whole program which was put into effect by the government during the war.
So much for what farm organizations think of the British contracts and what the people generally, and more particularly the cattle producers, think of the cattle embargo. The same question was discussed at Brockville, and I have read the resolution which was passed for immediate consideration., and another which will be considered further in what they have to say to us later. This whole policy, which yesterday was condemned as one of inflation-and we admit there has been a certain degree of inflation-is a policy which has been holding down the increase in the cost of living to the level indicated by the figures mentioned here yesterday, showing that our cost of living is only 77-7 per cent of the cost of living in the United States.

Now I would ask what effect the policy of selling our products to the British under contract throughout the war and since has had upon agriculture in this country. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition says it has resulted in a lessening of production. I presume that argument can be sound only if he thinks the prices of farm products have not been sufficiently high. But throughout his whole speech he argued that the cost of living is too high, and also that food is the most important element in the cost of living. Therefore he tries to ride both horses at the same time, and in the end does not prove anything as far as the public are concerned. There are a great many facts to be considered in connection with the matter. One is the fact that farmers are getting the highest prices they have ever received on practically all farm products other than grain, which I think is a reasonable answer.

Someone asks about farm implements. When one starts to talk about the cost of production, everything must be considered-. When everything is taken into consideration, the cost of production in Canada is 77-7 per cent of what it is in the United States.
My hon. friends would perhaps like to have some further statistics with regard to that matter. What do they show? They show that last year the farmers of Canada had a very high return from the sale of their farm
products-a high return which was very help- . ful to them. Someone has said they had a heavy crop; that is the very opposite of the fact. Last year there was one of the poorest crops the farmers right across Canada have had. They were poor in the east because they could not get their crop ini in the spring of the year; they were poor in the west because a month before harvest we had hot, scorching weather which reduced the yield from the farms of that area. Nevertheless we had a very high gross return last year from the sale of our farm products in Canada-$1,760 million. What is of far greater importance, we had the highest net return on our farm products in 1946 that we have ever had in Canada. And after all, the net return is the important thing-that is, the difference between the cost of production and the sales value of the commodities produced.
When one examines the statistics with regard to last year, he finds we had the highest net return from the sale of farm products across Canada that we have ever had in the history of the country. In other words, in relation to our cost of production our returns were higher than they ever were before. Well, with our gross return higher than ever before, with the exception of the year 1944, aud1 with our net return higher than ever before, $1,267,400,000, no one can come to this House of Commons and prove to us that the government has not seen to it that the returns to farmers should rise at least as much as the cost to farmers, taking all factors into consideration which could be effective in both respects.
So I say there is no reason why we should accept a resolution such as that moved in amendment by either one party or the other as condemning the position of our farm policy in Canada. But I would say this, that the letters and the resolutions and the telegrams I have read to the house indicate that the only people in Canada who are concerned about getting the Progressive Conservative party back into power in Canada on this question are the members of that party. The members of all other parties in the house are not anxious to have them back-and that includes all of us. Members on this side of the house certainly are not anxious to have them back.

And the only worry the farmers have is that they might get back into office. If they did, farmers would return to those conditions which the leader of the opposition so eloquently described in a speech delivered on another occasion in the early

.part of this session-and to which, under the rules, I cannot refer. That was a speech in which he indicated that we had a development in this country under previous Liberal governments which did result in great prosperity. People of Canada believe-certainly the farmers do-that they have a government today which has got for them the highest returns they have ever had; that they have a government today which has drawn a wider margin between their costs and their returns than has ever existed before, and thereby put them in a more favourable position than they had ever occupied previously. Realizing those things, their chief concern is that this government remain in power, to keep them in that favourable position. How do they expect the government to do it? They expect it to do it by keeping down the cost of production, for the time being at least. They expect the government to do it by stabilizing returns on farm products at reasonable levels, as long as possible-through contracts, if we can get them, and through providing the farmers by one means or another with greater purchasing power than they ever had before. They realize they have that now. And then, by guaranteeing floors, if prices should slip in the United States or other markets, they would expect that help through subsidies.
My hon. friend says that he does not know whether he is in favour of subsidies or not. I do not know why he put it into an amendment and asked this house to vote for it if he does not know whether he is in favour of it. However, the suggestion is there that we have subsidies. I ask him to read the policy of the Liberal party, to read it as expressed in the bill which was discussed fully in this house at a time prior to his being in it, a measure which is still on the statute book. The only resolution passed at Brockville the other day by the farm organizations in relation to that legislation was that we make it permanent. They said, ' This is one of the best things we have ever had; this is what we want but it covers only the transitional period; make it permanent." Any organization which asks this government to make permanent a policy which has been placed upon the statute books is not criticizing this government; it is criticizing every critic of this government.
I suggest that that act is a protection which we have under Liberal policy for the stabilization which is indicated in the contracts up to the present time and which, immediately we are not able to make contracts, will be taken care of by the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Two hundred million dollars are 
provided for products other than grain in order to make sure that the prices of those products will not fall to undue levels.
My hon. friend says, in supporting this policy which is stated here, that the price he thinks the farmers ought to have is the price they were getting in 1945. We have said in our contracts with Great Britain that the price we want as a floor price shall not be lower than the one which obtained for beef and pork in 1946, when prices were more than twenty per cent higher than they were in 1945. We went further and we placed upon the statute books of this country an act which makes it possible for us to subsidize in the interests of the basic agricultural industry of this country the production of products should prices in the United States market or elsewhere where we would naturally market our products find a lower level than should prevail.
Why did we do that? We did that because in 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944 and, following the act, in 1944, 1945, and 1946, we asked the farmers to be satisfied with a lower price than- they otherwise could have got. My hon. friends say, "Why do you put a ceiling price on butter? Why do you put a ceiling price on meat?" That is not the question they should be asking this house. The leader of the C.C.F. party stated the position in a manner which should confront the mind of every hon. member in this house. He said, 'Why did you put the price of butter so high?"
There is only one reason why the price of butter was put so high. It was done in order to make it impossible for our critics anywhere in Canada to say that after the farmer had delivered butter at from 48 to 55 cents a pound throughout the whole summer and provided1 it to the consumer at those price levels throughout the whole summer when he was producing twice as much butter as could be consumed in this country, when he was producing only half of what could be consumed or one-quarter of what 'had been produced in the summer he was forced back to a lower price level for a product which was being marketed in this country under the adverse weather conditions we have in winter from one end to the other. Instead of allowing a few people of the type described by the Prime Minister the other day, who are always prepared to take advantage of any condition, to make inordinate profits, a price would be set sufficiently high to give the farmer a reasonable return upon his product in winter when related to the fact that he had marketed at a low price during the summer months.

I want to say that if the same principle is applied to meat or anything else, it is not going to hurt the farmer. That principle protects the consumer against unduly high retail prices, but it does not take a single nickel out of the pockets of the farmers of this country. A policy which protects the consumer is sound because we have said in the prices support legislation that if the time ever comes when the bottom falls out of prices we will ask every taxpayer in this country to help to the extent provided in the Agricultural Prices Support Act, that is, $200 million, to maintain the price levels. If we are going to ask the taxpayers of Canada to do that, then this government must suggest to the producers that they should not expect to take full advantage of higher price levels which may obtain in the United States. We should keep control of our own position in Canada and see to it that the farmers are reasonably well paid for their production. At the same time we should see to it that the great mass of our people are kept in a frame of mind where they will maintain that legislation on the statute book.
I am not at all afraid that on the policies advocated a Conservative government may be here some day; I am not even afraid that a C.C.F. government may be here some day, but we should talk about this sufficiently often and long enough to convince the people of this country that no matter what government i3 here this is something the farmers want to continue at least until through maintenance of a reasonable relationship between costs and returns they have had back some of what they have contributed toward the maintenance of reasonable price levels in Canada during the last five or six years. If we do that there will be no necessity for the criticisms that were made yesterday by the leader of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has just delivered a speech which I can describe only as being a combination of political bombast and gross inaccuracy. The first part of that characterization speaks for itself, but I intend to prove the second part in the brief time at my disposal.
The first inaccuracy of which the Minister of Agriculture permitted himself to be guilty in an effort to discredit the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken) was contained in the statement made toward the end of his speech when he said that the agricultural policy of the leader of the opposition was to give farmers prices no higher than those which prevailed in 1945. That is refuted by
a reference to the very platform statement which the minister read at the opening of his speech. He has it there on his desk in front of him, and he will see by reference to it that the leader of the opposition said in his platform that the policies he advocated would result in agriculturists receiving an income at least twenty per cent above the levels they were receiving in 1945. That was his policy; it certainly was not to give them only the income they received in 1945.

If he is going to criticize that agricultural policy on the basis of that advertisement, he must stick to that advertisement. That advertisement shows that he has been guilty of inaccuracy.
The next inaccuracy-there is quite a long list-is that the Minister of Agriculture tried to leave the impression that the present policy advocated by the leader of the opposition would be opposed to firm contract prices -a permanent policy of forward contract prices were the words used in 1945. That, of course, is not an accurate statement of the facts. It is true that the leader of the opposition has repeatedly criticized the actual contracts made with the British government; but he has criticized them, not on the basis of their attempting to give stability to agricultural prices, but on the basis that the prices set fasten upon the Canadian farmer the burden of the national policy of providing food for Great Britain and Europe at less than world prices. The last inaccuracy of the minister was when he represented that all farmers are satisfied with the government, particularly with its agricultural policy, and want to see the present government continue in office. Whereas eight of the nine provinces of Canada have shown by their actions in passing provincial marketing legislation that, in their opinion, such legislation is necessary and in the public interest;

(1)	That this 1947 convention of the B.C. Federation of Agriculture again puts on record its belief that dominion marketing legislation, to supplement the provincial acts, is urgently necessary if the farmers of Canada are to be placed in a position equal to that of other elements in the community;

The minister said, for instance, that production costs in Canada were lower than in the United States, but prices of all industrial equipment in the United States would seem to challenge the accuracy of that statement.
However, not having the figures available just now to go further into that question I should like to revert to the main subject before the house at the moment, namely, the motion for the setting up of this committee to inquire into the increased cost of living. There is hardly any need to say that I share the belief expressed by other hon. members, that this step is not a forward step but only a side step; because, Mr. Speaker, surely no committee is needed at the moment to reveal the true facts of the situation, which are obvious to the Canadian people. These facts are that the rise in the cost of living is due, first, to the existence of shortages, and second, to government policies which increase inflation and make shortages more drastic.
With respect to the first cause of the increase in the cost of living, namely, shortages, of course our problem there is to increase production, because we have set ourselves the task of feeding not only Canada but the people of the United Kingdom and of Europe as well. Government policies, as has been shown by the leader of the opposition, have had the direct effect of discouraging production by maintaining controls on the price of one commodity, namely food, while allowing the cost of all items entering into the production of food to increase, with the result that production did not increase. In many fields it went down and the shortage of food has increased.
I think the people of Canada are prepared to recognize that, to a large extent, they have been living in the past off the depressed standard of one section of the community, namely the farmers. If the people of Canada are convinced that the farmer is now receiving a more adequate return for his work I do not believe that they will be inclined to question too much the justice of that situation. They do question it if they do not believe that the farmer is receiving a fair return, and I want to deal with that point shortly insofar as profiteering is concerned. (But in approaching this problem we should bear clearly in mind that the fact that production went down instead of going up because of the maintenance of controls on one group of commodities alone, is another illustration of a basic truth, namely, that controls to be effective must be 100 per cent. What we are seeing here, Mr. Speaker, is not so much a breakdown of the free enterprise system as a breakdown of the control system. It is not free enterprise which is having its last trial; it is control and managed economies, government planning, dictatorship, which have had their trial and have been found to be wanting.
I have not heard any member seriously question the statement of fact that controls
Prices Committee

to be effective must be 100 per cent. There are two methods by which one can increase production, and' control is certainly one of them. One hundred per cent control would work if you wanted it; hut we of the official opposition at least, do not want it. We have opposed it. Unlike the government, we have never advocated it. We realize, for instance, that control to be workable must be 100 per cent, and that means wage control. Wage control,	besides	being undesirable,	is
impossible; and even the members of the C C.F. party are not prepared' to fight on this ground, although they do ask for the reimposition of price control. The government also does not believe that price control is possible; but what a conversion we see there, a complete about-face. The government is now trying to climb on the band-wagon of free enterprise, and making a complete about-face, which should also be borne in mind when considering the true facts of the situation.
I should like at this point to mention some of the remedies that were indicated by the leader of the opposition. We say control will not work; but we do not say that there is no remedy, no steps which can be taken to deal positively with the increase in the cost of living. Amongst the remedies were, first, to take off the indirect and hidden taxes which directly increased the cost of living; instead of which the government, through the austerity program, the embargo program and excise taxes introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has added at least 25 per cent to the cost of living. The second step is to prosecute speculation where it is found to exist. The third step is to encourage production, especially on the farm; and the fourth step is to give free enterprise a chance, to have the will to see it work, to encourage it and allow it to work as it will to give us the highest standard of living in the whole world.
Let us see how the government treats these positive steps which can be taken to deal with the increase in the cost of living. Many government spokesmen have discussed the matter, but I want to refer to a speech which we heard last night, a speech which, with deference, I do not think offered any constructive approach to the problem. It seemed to me, as the heir apparent to the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke, that we saw a new Paul with a new message to the Gentiles. The message was that now he is a believer in free democracy and free enterprise, and especially in free enterprise. This new Paul made reference to a gibe which had been used about the leader 
of the opposition. He spoke of shifting to another political foot. I thought-what a strange knowledge of this "feat" is revealed by the minister in his present attitude; how very different the speech which he made last night was in its effect and in its purport from the speeches which he made when he was Minister of Justice in 1945. At that time he defended the very opposite point of view, and he jeered at and laughed at hon. members, especially of the official opposition, when we asked for the restoration of democracy, and freedom from undemocratic controls, freedom from regulation by order-in-council. We asked for the restoration of the rule of law and for the freedom of the ordinary businessman from the threat of arbitrary and dictatorial authority. Did the minister agree then? He certainly did not, as hon. members will see, if they read his speech delivered at the time. '
Speaking on this question on December 5, 1945, as reported at page 3000 of Hansard, referring to charges of dictatorial control, the minister said:
There _ seems to me something very unreal about this challenge as to there having been such dictatorial autocracy pushing people around in this country. If there was dictatorial autocracy m pushing people around, then we in the government are responsible for what was done, and we took that responsibility before the Canadian people.
_ Is there any attitude of belief in business integrity, belief in freedom of enterprise, in these remarks of the right hon. gentleman? What a change of political feet is there 1 It reminds us that the present Liberal government in this respect is something like a centipede; it has about a hundred political feet, and the heir apparent to the Prime 'Minister provides a good proportion of them.
Another about-face by the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in the matter of controls. Speaking in Quebec, as reported in the Quebec Chronicle Telegraph of January 12 of this year the minister said as follows:
Mr. St. Laurent went on record as being of the opinion that ceilings and controls on prices, wages and salaries were "neither possible, nor desirable in peacetime."
What a conversion! We find the minister saying the same thing in the house. He said in the house last night, as reported at page 773 of Hansard:
I still believe .that the institutions worked by reasonable-minded people can be worked in a reasonable way and that there are more men in business and in enterprise in Canada who want free enterprise 'to be worked in a reasonable way to the benefit of the whole community rather than of .the few who attempt to take advantage of any possible circumstances to extract inordinate prices.

Prices Committee
If he believes that, why then at Quebec a few days earlier does he speak as follows, and I am reading from a report of his speech appearing in the Montreal Gazette of January 12:
"But this provides the greedy'-and unfortunately they exist everywhere and always-the opportunity to find exorbitant profit cuts. There are greedy in all spheres ... .it is necesary to find means to bring them to reason."
"This is pressing," said Mr. St. Laurent, "and we know it is pressing. It becomes more urgent from day to day, almost from hour to hour. We know it and we are working on it."
What position does the right hon. gentleman really take? If the situation is so pressing; if there are in Quebec so many greedy and unscrupulous businessmen as he states, why then in the house some two weeks later does he say that he believes that there are far more right-minded and public-spirited businessmen than there are the opposite kind, and that free enterprise, if at last given a chance, will work? That is another change of political feet. Remember this, Mr. Speaker; if the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) believes as he says he does-and it is difficult to know what he does believe- that there is this degree of speculation, then why does he say only that they are working on it? Why does he not do something about it? Because in the house here he does not say it is urgent; that they are working on it, and are trying to find a way to deal with it, as he did in Quebec. On the contrary, in the house on February 2, as reported at page 772 of Hansard, he said:
It remained the law of this land that no one was entitled to charge for a commodity a price which was higher than that which was fair and reasonable.
So here we find the Secretary of State for External Affairs saying that we have power to deal with the matter, that we have the law now, which is quite a different thing from saying that we have to find a way to deal with it.
And remember further, Mr. Speaker, that in so far as speculation exists and is one of the causes of the increase in the cost of living, the government made it possible for speculation to exist. The first responsibility for speculation must be attached to the present government as a result of their saying that they would give an increase in prices and then waiting for two or three weeks to say what the increases were to be. thus encouraging speculators to hoard; and by producing uncertainty on the market inducing producers to hold back their marketing, thereby artificially increasing shortages and further aggravating inflation. I suggest, further, that all this talk of speculation and 5849-52J
profiteers, and prosecuting speculators and profiteers, is just a smoke screen, because there has not been a prosecution started although the law has been on the statute books of this country ever since 1939 and before that.
But I believe it is quite probable that there is some speculation. I think the people of the country believe that to be so. Some of the inquiries which have been made in the past, and some of the actions which we see at present, lead one to believe that there is speculation and that there may be profiteering, and so I should like to make a suggestion as to a method of dealing with that situation. I make it because I strongly believe that the free enterprise system is the best system and that it must be made to work. My suggestion would be that an amendment should be made to the criminal code of Canada which would provide that it shall be a criminal offence to make a mark-up or charge a profit of more than is just and reasonable under the circumstances; that the question of what is just and reasonable should be a question of fact for determination by a jury; and that amongst the considerations which the jury should bear in mind in- determining what is just and reasonable are, first, the costs of production or distribution and, second, the existence or otherwise of a national shortage of an essential commodity. I say that those are amongst the considerations, not that those are the only considerations.
In elaboration of this view I suggest that the problem once more is to reconcile liberty and security, to preserve freedom of action and freedom of opportunity on the one hand, and freedom from want and freedom from fear on the other. Surely it is possible for us to realize that all those who take part in these discussions are equally sincere and equally intent on achieving the good of their country. The position one takes depends upon which of the two aspects of freedom one happens to hold to be more essential-the preservation of initiative, opportunity and independence, or security and safety from economic dominance.
It is because we in the official opposition hold liberty so dear that stress has been laid on the importance of maintaining independence and of allowing private judgment, private initiative and private discretion to function freely in place of government regulation. Liberty is a delicate flower of glorious proportions and strong colouring, but reaching its most perfect development when allowed to bloom freely in the open sunshine; too easily is it choked, especially in its early growth, by the clinging vines of regulation and restriction. Furthermore, while the plant of regulation
Prices Committee

and restriction, in its early stages, may provide a readier and more comfortable staff of support than the more delicate and rarer bloom of liberty, still, if unchecked, the former will be found to develop into a choking parasite, sapping the parent body of all strength and vigour, and eventually choking out all true life; while liberty will be found only to provide a constantly increasing source of strength and inspiration, of alternate light and shade, in the midst of which life can develop to its fullest and most vigorous realization.
If this then be the picture, or an approximation of it, it is liberty that, above all, must be cultivated and protected. There are many who hold this view; and the socialists in particular are, of course, guilty of gross misrepresentation when they say we resist government control in order to enable our friends to make a profit. However, not all Canadians are so deliberately blind in one eye as are the hon. members of the C.C.F. party. Those who see out of both eyes realize that, in the preservation of liberty, there are other dangers to be faced than that of government control. One of them is, undoubtedly, economic greed, the greed which carries freedom of action to the point where it becomes not liberty but license, because it constitutes a trespass upon someone else's freedom.
Believing that the preservation of liberty is essential to the public good and recognizing that liberty is as much in danger from excessive private control as from excessive public control, I suggest that the truly democratic solution, the solution most acceptable to a free people, is in letting the people themselves determine the limitations to be imposed on their own freedom. I do nob believe any expert, controller or board can or should tell us what is the limit of freedom.
If a jury of twelve men is asked to decide in any case whether a profit or mark-up is reasonable, you will get people who may themselves later be affected by their own decision by being in the same circumstances. That is the fairest kind of decision. Here it should be remembered that if we entrust to a jury the determination of w'hether or not a man has been guilty of murder-a decision which carries with it life or death-if we are willing to leave that question of fact to be determined by a jury, then surely, having confidence in our system -of justice and the fairness of our Canadian people, we can safely leave to their determination the question of whether or not a profit is just and reasonable. Furthermore, by this means the great principle of responsibility is maintained. The individual must decide for himself whether his price is fair and just, and all that is imposed upon
rMr. Fulton.]
him is the additional responsibility of bearing in mind the public good as well as his own private interest. Actually this responsibility is always present and rests upon us all in our capacity as citizens. By this means, however, by this amendment of the criminal code we give to each individual the opportunity to enforce his rights instead of leaving everything to the state, and we also lay on the entrepreneur, the man in business, the man who controls an industrial machine the duty to exercise his responsibility.
I for one, Mr. Speaker, believe that by some such device private enterprise can be made responsible. If it is made responsible, it is so manifestly superior to any other system that its survival and the survival of liberty are ensured. If it is not made responsible, not only will the people as a whole continue to suffer, but I believe irresponsibility will inevitably lead to the overthrow of the system, and with it true freedom and independence will perish from the earth.
Another method advocated by the official opposition of checking the increase in the cost of living is the removal of indirect taxes. This matter also was referred to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs last evening, and again he showed- a remarkable facility in shifting from one political foot to the other. Not only in matters of policy did he depart from the traditional line of the Liberal party, but he attempted to ridicule the suggestion put forward by the leader of the opposition by what I would term an unworthy reference to some particular indirect taxes, namely those on spirits and tobacco, and to imply that the leader of the opposition had those taxes in mind when he demanded the removal of indirect taxes. That suggestion is so unworthy and so far-fetched that I am not going to deal with it in particular, but I want to refer to the minister's view as it must be gathered from his approach to this question of indirect taxes in general. Certainly from what he said it can be inferred that he felt that indirect taxes are not a burden on the people; that all one has to do to avoid paying them is not to buy, and therefore they should remain. Well, that is in direct opposition to the view held and expressed by his present leader, and I suggest that perhaps the right hon. gentleman would be better advised to wait until he is actually the leader before he tries to substitute his own views for the expressed policy of his party. However, that is a matter for my hon. friends opposite to determine.
In this respect I wish to quote from a statement made by the Prime Minister, what I take to be the official view of that party.

Prices Committee
Here, of course, one has to bear in mind that there are two different outlooks with respect to quotations from the Prime Minister. One view is that he is the ultimate authority on any problem. That view is, of course, held largely and vigorously by those who sit around and behind him. But we must bear in mind that the Prime Minister is a many-sided man, and there are others who hold the view that the authority which otherwise would be inherent in quotations of his words is somewhat lessened by the fact that generally he can be quoted on the other side as well. Be that as it may, however, I want to quote from his remarks when he was definitely and unequivocally in favour of a reduction of indirect taxes. He was speaking in this house in 1920, during a somewhat similar period, and was criticizing the government for failing to deal with the rising cost of living. As reported at page 2977 of Hansard for June 1, 1920, the present Prime Minister said:
Sir, I wish also to say that another reason for our exception to the budget is that it reveals the outstanding fact that the government has no policy for dealing with the high cost of living . . . We could not expect hon. gentlemen opposite to solve that question. Certainly not; hut we at least had a right to expect that they would take some step towards a solution of the problems which the high cost of living involves, and that they would have had some suggestion to offer which would, if adopted, have helped to relieve the burdens which men, women and children in this country are bearing today.
I might pause here to observe that the appointment of a parliamentary committee can hardly be held up as a constructive step which will result in relieving the burden the people have to bear today. Then the Prime Minister went on:
But what have they done? Instead of alleviating the high cost of living as it affects the great mass of consumers, they have added to it. They have increased the cost of living and made it more difficult for the people of Canada to live than it has been heretofore. To an invisible tariff they have added a visible tariff on a great multitude of commodities, .thereby *increasing the cost of living to the vast body of consumers. From one end of Canada to_ the other, in every home, there has .been considerable difficulty in coping with the situation . . . As I say, Mr. Speaker, instead of meeting the high cost of living as it was obviously the duty of the government to have met it, by reducing the tariff on the necessaries of life, they have added this visible tariff in the nature of an excise to the invisible .tariff .which already exacts its toll from the people in regard to commodities in general use.
Could there be a more perfect parallel? The present government, headed by the right hon. gentleman whom I have quoted here in 1920, adds to the already burdensome cost of living in 1948 a further increase of twenty-five per cent in excise taxes on many basic commodities.
In the same speech the Prime Minister said, in reference to indirect taxes in general, as reported at page 2980 of Hansard for the same date:
It is turn-over that counts-and the greater the number of transactions the better it will be for the man who is fortunate enough to be carrying on a particular business. Now what is the effect of the taxation which the government is proposing? It is for the most part in the nature of a restriction upon trade; it is making it more difficult for those engaged in trade and commerce to carry on . . .
Then the final quotation is as follows, at page 2898:
Now, sir, let me speak more particularly in reference to the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) which is before the house. Unless I have altogether failed in making apparent what I believe to be most necessary in this country at the present time, not only because of Canadian needs but because of the .world situation today, it will be evident that above all else we should have a policy which will help reduce the high cost of living and increase production.
And he went on to say:
... its whole aim .and purpose is to call upon the government to take immediate steps here and now to relieve the problem of the high cost of living by reducing the duties on the necessities of life *. . .
That was the view of the Prime Minister in 1920, and I do not understand why the leader apparent, the leader elect, should hold an opposite view in 1948 and should say, in regard to the reduction of indirect taxes, that this is a light matter, not to be seriously considered.
In conclusion I would recommend to the consideration of the house and of the country that the cost of living would be better dean with by adopting the policies put forward by the leader of the opposition yesterday than by having this parliamentary committee.

Definitely. It is not a matter of one's years; it is a matter of the terms in which one thinks. I did, however, listen with interest to the plea he made for free enterprise. He believes in free enterprise; he believes in it even if he has to maintain it by amendments to the criminal code. That was the first thing he proposed, to make free enterprise work.
They have been trying to make it work for ages. Free enterprise, when, it is absolutely free, is tyranny of the very worst kind. A large part of the work of democratic assemblies since the beginning of the industrial revolution has been attempts to humanize free enterprise. I would ask anyone who does not believe that to read the industrial history of England, to read the fight that was made in that country; and then I would ask him to read of the efforts to that end in this country.
I have before me the report of a-committee of which the majority were members of the Conservative party. I admit that the report was made before the Conservative party became Progressive. However, I would not put that forward as a reason .for my hon. friend's not giving some thought or some study to it. I refer, of course, to the report of the price spreads and mass buying committee and commission of 1934, and I would draw the hon. members attention to page 264, at which the conclusions are set out. They are:
1.	That in certain industries, such as public utilities, monopoly control requires complete regulation or government ownership.
2.	That in certain other industries competition can be satisfactorily restored by state action.
3.	That in some imperfectly competitive industries the attempts to restore competition must be supplemented at least by some sort of maximum price control, profit restriction, or other method of regulation.
i. That in other industries where simple competition is operative, such competition may continue to be relied upon as the best method of control.
That is, where competition is operative. It continued:
5. And that, finally, there may be a few industries in which competition has become so cutthroat that some modification of it may be attempted, or permitted.

And if we turn to the end of the report, we find this:
We recommend, that is to say, not only the most complete maintenance or restoration of competition, where that is possible, but also gradual, progressive and effective regulation in that growing field of business enterprise wrhere monopoly or imperfect competition will continue inevitably to develop, and, if unregulated, will continue to exploit the primary producer, the wage earner and the consumer in the shameful ways so often disclosed by the evidence before us. We propose the first steps to the goal that has been well described as "'the socialization of monopoly and the civilization of competition." Unless we can achieve this goal in the reasonably near future, there well may be forced upon us changes in our economic, social, and political organization beside which our proposals, important as we believe them to be, will pale into insignificance.
Let me tell my hon. friend that those changes have not come about in the fourteen years since that report was submitted to the House of Commons. It is because you cannot at the same time control free enterprise and leave it free. We must organize the social and industrial institutions of the country so that their purpose will be to contribute to the welfare of the people of the country.
I have another reference on free enterprise which I should like to read to my hon. friends to my right. When the Labour party came into office in Great Britain in 1945, Mr. Churchill referred to it as a temporary aberration on the part of the people. Lord Woolton, who was food controller in the coalition government during the war, and is now, I believe, chairman of the Conservative party in Great Britain, thinks differently-and he is very candid about it.
An article quoting him in the Daily Herald of London, December 18, 1947, says this:
Socialism-
And my hon. friend referred to socialists.
Socialism is the alternative to the form of industrial life we have practised in this country in the past, and has arisen as a protest against the conduct rather than the principles of free enterprise. It has gained its early supporters from men who either themselves have been the victims, or have seen their families the victims, of a system that placed human values behind material gain. We have indeed reaped a whirlwind.

As I say, those are merely contributory factors which have become possible because of the basic factor of shortages combined with effective demand. These inflationary factors became apparent very early in the war. The government felt that under the then existing conditions uncontrolled prices would endanger the war effort and prompt and effective steps were taken to control prices. Those regulations remained effective so long as they were maintained; but with the end of hostilities a clamour arose for the removal of controls, for the end of government by bureaucracy. That clamour started among the business people of the country and it was echoed on the hustings and in this house by the Progressive Conservatives.
Let me say that the inflation and the high prices we have today did not come upon us by stealth in the night. We could see them coming because, as each control was removed, the prices of the goods in the sector covered by that particular control shot upwards. As each subsidy was discontinued the same thing happened. To ask this House of Commons to set up a committee to find out what is the cause of the high cost of living is a reflection on the intelligence of the members of this house. Everybody knows it, and the only reason we are asked to investigate it now is to provide some means by which the government can be saved from the embarrassment of having to answer the letters and resolutions they are receiving in regard to the matter.
As I say, this did not come upon the government by stealth. They were made aware of what was happening even if they could not see it themselves. It was right under their eyes. This group at least warned the government time and time again. I could cite numerous instances, but I shall satisfy myself with citing one which occurred in this house on April 14, 1947, not quite a year ago. At that time a speech was made by the leader of this group, I think on a motion to go into supply, in which he said:
We have all come back fresh from the country. Some hon. members have been to their constituencies, and others have moved around in different parts of Canada. What we have found over the last several weeks should cause this house a good deal of concern. The people of Canada are worried as perhaps they have not been worried for a very long time.
Let me say that if they were worried in April of last year, they are doubly worried in February of this year.
I met a good many who were worried about how they are going to make ends meet during the next few months or the next year. I am not dealing specifically with the question of controls; I am dealing with the cost of living. The sharp increases in the cost of living to the
Prices Committee

people of Canada are causing misgivings in the minds of those who are responsible for the family budgets.
That was ten months ago, almost a year. That worry, that fear, that inability to provide for the family is much greater today than it was in April, 1947.
At the end of his speech my leader moved the following resolution, seconded by myself, and it will be found at page 2008 of Hansard:
This house desires to record its opinion that the government should give consideration to the immediate restoration of price control on and lower prices for the necessaries of life, particularly articles of food and clothing, shelter, household appliances, and supplies and machinery needed by the farmers in connection with their work;
Further, this house is of the opinion that the harmful and dangerous effects of the rising cost of living demand immediate and effective action."
That was on April 14, 1947, and on February 2, 1948, the Prime Minister became so seized of the situation caused by rising prices that he moved for a committee to be set up to investigate it.
I said that the C.C.F. alone of all parties in this house kept drawing attention to the dangers inherent in rising prices and the removal of controls. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), as reported at page 768 of Hansard made a statement yesterday which I cannot allow to pass without some reply. He said:
I wish to make it abundantly clear once and for all, Mr. Speaker, that this group believes controls are necessary to a reduction in the cost of living. We have always taken that position; and anyone who goes out on the 'hustings and says we have taken any other position is definitely lying.
I happen to be one, Mr. Speaker, who has said differently. I do not knowingly lie, and if I lied in this matter I am going to leave it to the house to say whether I had justification or not. I am going to quote from what my hon. friend the member for Peace River said in this house on March 21, 1947. At page 1606 of Hansard he said:
It must be increasingly evident to all thinking Canadians that we have to get away from our present methods of doing some things. We all must admit that. Surely every straightthinking Canadian can see that it is the harsh taxation, the centralized state controls, the state imposed restrictions and the bureaucratic regimentations introduced under war conditions that have landed Great 'Britain, _ the United States and Canada into the mess in which we are floundering today.
Surely my hon. friend, after making that diagnosis of the condition of Canada, would not support controls.
