He deplored the fact that price controls had been scrapped so hastily while the economy was still greatly affected by wartime influences.
The mistake-and I mentioned it in the house before-we made at the end of hostilities was that when the fighting was at an end we thought the effects of the war were also at an end, and that all we had to do was to rush back and start where we had been before, each one trying to get as much as possible for himself without any regard for the other fellow. That is free enterprise, and it has got us in the jam in which we now are.

I brought into the chamber with me a file containing thirty-five or forty letters and resolutions, and there is not a single one which asks for the setting up of a committee. I have several letters and resolutions from branches of the Canadian Legion dealing with the high cost of living and its effect on members of the legion. What the people want who write me is for the government to do something that will help them out of their present difficulty. They do not want an investigation. They know what is wrong as far as they are concerned; they know they just cannot buy the things that they need. They also have the feeling that since the government could and did maintain prices at a proper level so that they could buy these things during the war, the government can do so now.
My right hon. friend- said that this was a fact-finding committee, and he spoke of the importance of finding facts. In reply to that I should like to give him the answer he made to the leader of the government of the day when the resolution setting up the price spreads committee was adopted. It will be found on page 191 of Hansard, 1934, and reads as follows:
There is one other aspect which I think is perhaps even more important. It is that the government has already legislation available to deal with matters of this kind, if it will view -the whole question sympathetically. Legislation is one thing, but the administration of existing law is quite another.
I submit the government has all the power necessary to deal with this situation and, as the Prime Minister said in 1934, the government can use the staff of combines investigation branch to investigate. If that was good advice in 1934 it is ten times better advice today because the combines investigation branch has been greatly improved and enlarged and the law under which it operates has been strengthened since 1934. But in addition to the combines investigation branch staff, we now have the staff of the wartime prices and trade board, and if both of these were working together they could quickly ascertain the facts in the situation, because they know where to look for the facts much better than a parliamentary committee does.
I suggest again that what the people of this country want is an easing of their difficulties. The people on small, fixed incomes, the unorganized workers, who are feeling the brunt of high prices, want an easing of their difficulties. The people in the middle and higher income brackets do not feel the pinch of the high cost of living to the same extent. Its effect on them is that it causes them to do less luxury buying or less saving; consequently it does not affect their standard of living. The standard of living of the people I mentioned a moment ago, those in the low-income groups,

is seriously and adversely affected, and I suggest that what is required is not a parliamentary committee but action by the government.

speechtext:
I have been thinking about the amendment which was introduced by the leader of the opposition, and it occurred to me that there was perhaps some confusion in the minds of the mover and the seconder of that amendment with regard to the meaning of the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Then, when I found the amendment to the amendment put in, it seemed to me that there was reason for believing that both the amendment and the subamendment were out of order; and I shall submit to you that such is the case, on several grounds. I cannot in just a word express the objection I have to make to you, Mr. Speaker; but in effect it is, that in the first place-but not solely on this ground-this amendment which is moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) changes the whole nature of the resolution of the Prime Minister. I cannot better lay before you and the house the general idea than by drawing your attention to a ruling which will be found at page 696 of Beauchesne's third edition. I would ask leave to read part of that, because a considerable part of what I shall say from then on will be more or less a commentary upon a set of facts similar to those which were involved in that ruling. That ruling was given upon a quite similar motion to set up a committee to deal with redistribution, which I am sure Your

Prices Committee
Honour will recall. On March 13, 1939, it had been moved by Mr. Power that a special committee consisting of So-and-so and So-and-so should be set up to study and report upon the following subjects:
(a) Methods used to effect a redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and in other countries and to make suggestions to the house in conneotion therewith.
The committee was to report upon the redistribution. Then, on the question being proposed, Mr. Pelletier moved and Mr. Fair seconded an amendment which read as follows:
In order to facilitate the carrying out of instructions contained in paragraph "B" of the resolution, have power to investigate 'the amounts of contributions held at various times by various federal political parties, or party assistants on behalf of such parties . . .
And so on. From as much as I have read, you will see that the amendment then offered was changing the whole nature of the motion, and that was the ruling of the Speaker:
Mr. Speaker ruled the amendment out of order on the ground that it raised a new question not contemplated by the notice of motion as the said amendment proposed to extend the powers of the committee far beyond those set down in the notice, and that the necessity of giving notice will be superseded if such notice is not used as a guidance for the decision of the house.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the situation here. If one might shortly describe the motion of the Prime Minister, it might be said to be a motion to set up a committee by means of which light can be thrown into dark places. It is not any more than just the turning of light on this problem of high prices. It is a fact-gathering committee that it is the desire to have set up. I am not speaking as to the merits or demerits of the motion itself, but am only shortly describing it in that fashion.
Then we come to the amendment of the leader of the opposition, and in addition .to the (a), (b) and (c), the pants of the motion of the Prime Minister which direct that this shall be a fact-gathering committee, we find that the leader of the opposition is introducing (d), (e) and (f) to change the nature of the committee entirely from a fact-finding committee 'to a committee that will express opinions, possibly its own. What is much more serious than that, this committee would in effect be the cabinet rather than a committee of this house, because now, under .the proposals of the leader of the opposition, its duties are to advise on government policy. If this were accepted, we would have changed the whole constitutional basis of government by substituting for the cabinet form of government, government by committee, a form of government with which wTe in Canada are
quite familiar in view of the fact that we see it in operation day by day south of the international boundary. Apparently it is a usual method in the United States to set up a committee, have it make recommendations upon any subject whatever, and then have those recommendations considered by congress. But I submit that that procedure is quite foreign to the parliamentary system of this country. Government policy is to be designed by that committee which we commonly call the cabinet, which has that responsibility and which must at all times have the confidence of the House of Commons. That in itself seems to me sufficient to require that a ruling should be given denying .the validity of the amendment of the leader of the opposition.
But if we go a little farther than that we might say that, in addition to changing the whole nature of .the committee, there are parts of the resolution of the leader of the opposition which are quite unnecessary by reason of the terms of the original motion to set up the committee. For example, if you will disregard for a moment the fact that paragraph
(d)	of the amendment makes a statement of fact respecting effective government policy on rising prices, and just consider that the paragraph directs the committee to study facts with .particular relevance to agricultural production, you would find that this is adequately taken care of already by paragraph (a) of the original resolution of the Prime Minister.
Then again the proposals for subsidies, and the suggestion in both the amendment and1 the subamendment that there should1 be examination into the results of the discontinuance of subsidies-all	that is comprehended by paragraph (a) of the Prime Minister's resolution, which states that inquiry should be made into the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living. By reason of these points being already covered, I submit that the amendment is out of order on that ground also.
Then., when you come to look at paragraph (d) and some of the others you find that they make definite statements of fact. They are affirmations first and only incidentally directions to a committee which is to be charged with certain inquiries. For example, paragraph (d) deals with "the effect of present government policies in lessening Canadian agricultural production". If that were not a statement of fact it would be worded somewhat differently. Perhaps it would be worded like this: "the effect of government policies, and whether or not they have hadl some influence in1 lessening Canadian agricultural production". As it is, this paragraph states a fact. If this house sends that particular
Prices Committee

clause to a committee, then this house will be saying to the committee, "It is a fact that government policies have had1 such and such effect, and you are directed to inquire"-into what? The committee will not inquire into that fact, because it will have been predetermined by the house. What will the committee look into? Apparently the only answer there would be the extent to which these policies have had that effect which the judgement of the house has already determined to be a fact. There, I submit, is reason enough for ruling this entire amendment out of order. I think everyone will realize that the proper way to introduce any such statement is as a direct motion of want of confidence, and have it debated on the issue of whether or not the agricultural policies of the government have had that effect. That would be the proper way to approach it, instead of seeking an indirect vote of want of confidence which would be something like the periscope of a submarine coming up from below and never seen until it was too late.
There is something further in reference to both the amendment and the subamendment which I submit to Your Honour is very serious indeed. In addition to the fact that these amendments would direct the committee to be a policy-making body, thereby usurping the functions of the cabinet, they seek to put the committee in the position of recommending expenditures of public money. That will be seen in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, where it states that the committee is to report upon and recommend as to the advisability of continuing the present controls-and we cannot have the present controls without the expenditure of public money-and the advisability of reverting to the payment of subsidies, which, of course would also mean the payment of public money. A committee making a recommendation of that kind would be a body, not charged with the responsibilities of government, taking on the functions of government even to the extent of dipping into the public purse and directing expenditures therefrom.
The objections I am now expressing in reference to the amendment itself apply even more strongly to the subamendment which, in addition to speaking of measures to stem the rising cost of living, asks that recommendations should be made with respect to the restoration of price controls and subsidies. All this, I submit, shows that these amendments are not designed only to give direction to a fact-finding body, but are designed to change the fact-

finding body completely, making it a body which would have power to bring in recommendations on all manner of things, many of which could be relatively distant from the actual question of prices themselves, and very far afield from the original motion.
My reason for emphasizing this point is that this was the precise objection raised to the amendment offered by Mr. Pelletier and Mr. Fair to the motion moved by Mr. Power respecting redistribution. The ruling might be expressed in this way: the Speaker said something which had been proposed by Mr. Power, while left in the motion as before, had been so greatly changed as to be almost unrecognizable. In effect that is what we have here; a motion to set up a committee is so changed in the instance we are considering at the moment that this fact alone, I submit, would be reason for the amendments to be declared out of order. When you add the fact that under these amendments the committee would be made almost a cabinet, or at least a policy-making body, and in addition a body which would have power to recommend large expenditures of public money without the responsibility of administering those expenditures, then I submit there can be no question that both amendments are out of order.
I have no doubt there are other grounds upon which these amendments should be ruled out of order, but it would seem to me that "what I have said is sufficient to justify such a ruling. I do not know whether Your Honour would desire to deal with my point of order at the moment, but before the debate goes farther I should think the validity of these two amendments should be considered, whenever Your Honour is prepared to do so.

speechtext:
On the point of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank), I should like to submit to Your Honour that the amendment is in order. The hon. gentleman has taken twenty minutes to elaborate his argument in an endeavour to show the Speaker of the house why the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) should be ruled out of order. Your Honour will bear in mind at the outset that you are being asked to rule out of order an amendment which was introduced yesterday afternoon, and which has already been debated for the past twenty-four hours. An amendment has been offered to that amendment; and it is only now that objection is taken to the validity of the original amendment.

Prices Committee
In the first place, citation 112 as it appears at page 55 of Beauchesne's third edition, reads thus:
A point of order against procedure must be raised promptly .and before the question has passed to a stage at which the objection *would be out of place.
In my submission, the stage at which the objection, should have been taken, if indeed objection could properly be taken, certainly was before the amendment to the amendment was submitted. But objection, was not taken promptly and, in my submission, it is now too late. That, in itself, it seems to me is sufficient to dispose of the point raised by the hon. member.
But, dealing with the merits of his objection, I should like to submit to Your Honour that the hon. member does not bring the present case within the scope of the ruling made by 'Mr. Speaker Casgrain in 1939, as it is set forth at page 696 of Beauchesne's, third edition. I should like to draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that Mr. Speaker Casgrain ruled the amendment at that time out of order on the ground that it introduced an entirely new question. That is the essence of the ground upon which his ruling proceeded. But that is not the case in connection with the present question before Your Honour.
The effect of the original motion then before Mr. Speaker Casgrain was to appoint a committee to study and to report upon two classes of subjects. The first was the-
. . . methods used to effeot a redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and in other countries and to make suggestions to the house in connection therewith.
May I interject here that it is simply the question of redistribution.
The second subject was the-
. . . methods whereby (i) the source and disposition of sums received and expended in promoting the return of members of the House of Commons may be readily traceable; (ii) publicity may be given to all receipts and expenditures in connection therewith; (iii) the cost of elections to candidates may be reduced; (iv) the amount that may be spent by or on behalf of a candidate in his election campaign may be limited.
It will be observed there that the second class of subjects related to money received by candidates and expended by candidates in the course of an election campaign.
The amendment which was introduced to that motion to refer these questions to a committee chosen for the purpose was in these terms:
That the motion be amended by inserting the following words immediately after the words "special committee" in the first line of the last paragraph of the motion.
Then these are the words which it was proposed should be inserted:
In order to facilitate the carrying out of instructions contained in paragraph ".B" of the resolution, have power .to investigate the amounts of contributions held at various times by various federal political parties, or party assistants on behalf of such parties, in Canada, for the past ten years, the sources from which such contributions came and the dispositions from such contributions of all sums of $100 or over.
Let me draw attention to the fact that the subject matter of the amendment was contributions made to political parties, not to candidates, which was the subject matter of the original motion. On the contrary, it had to do with payments made to political parties. Whereas the subject matter of the original motion was payments to political candidates in the course of the election campaign, the subject matter of the amendment was contributions made to various political parties in Canada over a period of ten years.
It does not require any elaboration in order to see at once how utterly distinct the subject matter of the amendment was from that of the original motion. Therefore it was only to be expected that Mr. Speaker Casgrain would rule as he did, that the amendment was out of order on the ground that-
. . . it raised a new question not contemplated by the notice of motion as the said amendment proposed to extend the powers of the committee far beyond those set down in the notice.
That is not a case comparable with the one now before us. What Your Honour has here is, in my submission, an original motion which, if it means what it has been represented to the house to mean, would set up a committee to conduct a thorough and searching examination into the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living, prices which have been raised above justifiable levels, and increases in prices due to the acquisition by persons or the holding by persons of supplies.
The amendment introduced by the leader of the opposition bases itself firmly upon that foundation. It does not subtract anything from the original motion, and proceeds to indicate certain definite matters into which the committee ought to examine and concerning which it should report. It follows the same language-"examine and report upon".
I submit to Your Honour that the matters enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs (d),
(e), (f) and (g) of the amendment of the leader of the opposition are completely germane to the subject matter of the original motion to set up the committee.
(d) "The effect of present government policies in lessening Canadian agricultural production"-that has been put before Your

Prices Committee

Honour-and, I submit, rightly so-as one of the causes of the rising cost of living. That is the subject matter of paragraph (a) of the original motion. Then, in the amendment we find the following as paragraph (e) :
the advisability of continuing the present controls on prices of farm products. . .
And so on. Obviously this ties in with (d). And if (d) is in order, as I submit it is, then (e) is also in order. Then paragraph (f):
the -advisability of reverting to payment of subsidies on essential commodities of consumption.
Obviously that is tied in directly wjth the subject matter of (e). Then, (g):
spreads between -prices received by producers and prices paid by consumers.
That has a most direct bearing on the subject matter of paragraph (c) of the original motion.
In a word, the amendment of the leader of the opposition is completely germane to the subject matter of the original motion. The leader of the opposition has not introduced what was called by Mr. Speaker Casgrain in 1939 a new question; it is not a new question at all. It is the same question, but with several facets which have not been properly set forth in the original motion, and which are clearly brought forth in the amendment in order that the committee may not fail to perform the duties it must perform, if it is to have any significance whatsoever.
The final point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is that the committee may conceivably make recommendations which will relate to the expenditure of public money. It is quite conceivable that the original motion might lead to reports on the part of the committee which would relate to the expenditure of public money. I submit that the hon. member has overlooked that in the argument he addressed to Your Honour. In any event, the fact that the report of the committee may relate to the expenditure of public money does not, of itself, make it out of order, or put it beyond the powers of the committee to report. The house can, I submit, instruct the committee to bring in a report on those matters if it wishes.
In any event, whether it does or does not, the hon. member has no right to ask that Your Honour rule the amendment out of order on the ground that he is prepared1 now to anticipate that the committee may make recommendations which, when they are submitted to the house, may then be found to be out of order. That is no ground, in my submission, for ruling out of order at this stage an amendment which is not of itself, and on its face, necessarily out of order on that ground. That would be a ground for a ruling

in the committee by the chairman or, if the chairman failed in his duty, for a ruling by the Speaker when the committee had submitted its report to the house. The hon. member has no right to ask you to anticipate now that the committee will make recommendations beyond the proper powers given to it. I submit that the amendment introduced by my leader is entirely in order.

Mr. Speaker, I should
like to say a word before you give your ruling, and I assure you that I shall not be as long as the other two speakers who have spoken. As I understand it, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) has raised two -points of order. One is that the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) raises matters not related to the subject matter of the main motion. In regard to that I am in absolute agreement with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who contends that the proposals made by the leader of the opposition are absolutely germane to the subject matter of the main motion. Beauchesne's, second edition, citation 394, reads:
A motion may be amended: (a) -by -leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
That is exactly what the leader of the opposition did in his amendment. He added words which expanded to some extent the purpose of the motion moved by the- Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
The -other objection is that in the latter part of the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition it is stated that the committee may make recommendations to the House of Commons, and so on. It is said that would make the committee a policymaking committee. It does not do anything of the kind. The committee reports to the house; I suppose the government would not take cognizance of such a report until the house had dealt with it, and even then the government might not deal with it. It is nothing new for a committee to make recommendations. If I remember correctly, the committee on public accounts recommended last year that a royal commission be appointed to look into certain activities of the custodian of enemy alien property. That commission was set up and it is carrying on today. If I had a moment or two to look up the sessional papers I know I could give dozens of examples where committees -have made recommendations. Surely, if a committee has no power to make recommendations it has no power at all.

Prices Committee
In my opinion, there is nothing, either in the amendment or in the amendment to the amendment, that is contrary to the subject matter of the motion.
In closing, may I say that it is indicative of the freedom that is to be given to this committee that a member of the committee rises at this time to attempt to curtail the scope of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two with respect to this point of order and, since I am not a lawyer it will not be possible for me to take as much time as that taken by the first two speakers. Also I do not intend to open Beauehesne's. I have been sitting in the house for a number of years and I have listened to a good deal of argument in respect to what is in order and what is out of order. I must confess that, as I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg Soulh Centre (Mr. Maybank), I could not avoid thinking that he had laboured tremendously in trying to prove these amendments out of order. Of course I am reminded of the mountain that groaned, but I have not yet been able to detect what it brought forth.
I do not think the argument that the amendment to the amendment should be ruled out of order because it involves the expenditure of money can be taken seriously. No committee has ever been set up by parliament which did not carry with it an expenditure of money, because under the original motion committees are able to send for persons and papers and engage counsel. That all involves the expenditure of money. Surely my hon. friend had to labour that point.
He suggested also that this was merely a fact-finding committee, that it was a committee set up to let the light shine in dark places. But then the hon. member attempted to turn off the light and pull down the blinds. All the amendments attempt to do is to clarify the work of the committee, to give it instructions as to where t>he dark places are and where we want the light to shine in.
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is serious with respect to this committee he will want all light to shine in that it is possible to have shine. Surely arguments of this kind and an attempt to circumscribe and cramp the style of the committee are not what the Prime Minister told us the other day was the intent of the original motion. I maintain that, with the application of a little horse sense you will come to the right decision and rule the amendments in order.

It is merely giving instructions to the committee that it shall carry out in a certain way what the notice of motion desires. I submit that this amendment in no way interferes with the powers of the committee. I would call your attention to the fourteenth edition of May's Parliamentary Practice, page 516, where it is said:
Any amendment moved to an instruction must he strictly relevant thereto and must be drawn in such a way that, if accepted, the question as amended would retain the form and effect of an instruction.
The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition simply gives instructions.

speechtext:
I wish to draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that the two Progressive Conservative members who have spoken agree that the decision given by Mr. Speaker Casgrain in the case referred to was a sound one, namely, that if a proposed amendment raised a new question not contemplated by the notice of motion that would make the amendment out of order. I would emphasize the importance of that word "contemplated"-a new question not contemplated in the motion. I ask Your Honour to consider how this house is to decide what was contemplated in the motion. There are two ways of deciding that. One is by the wording of the motion itself, which is very clear. It gives powers for the purpose of fact finding in regard to the matters mentioned therein. The other is by the statement of the government itself as to what was contemplated by the motion when the motion was brought forward. I thought I made it very clear to the house that the government wished to avoid this committee becoming one that would enter into endless discussions of various matters, waste its time by trying to make policies, and that, for this reason, we had purposely left out at this stage any reference to the committee's powers to make recommendations. In speaking on the motion, I added that if, later on, the committee thought it advisable to have, in addition, powers to make recommendations, the government would be prepared to consider that recommendation and that I for one would be prepared to consider it favourably. I drew attention particularly to the fact that what the government wanted in this matter was action, not discussion; that what we wanted were the facts, not generalities and suggestions and theories and policies; that for that reason this particular motion had been shorn on the one side of any directions to the committee to bring in recommendations at this stage, and on the other side it was specifically limited to
Prices Committee

finding or gathering facts in regard to the rise in prices and the increased cost of living. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the purport, the intention, the nature of the motion would be changed were all the additional obligations set forth in the amendments allowed to be thrown upon the committee. That would just help to defeat what the government had in mind in proposing the committee in the terms it did, and what it believes the people of Canada want today, namely, to know whether some of the allegations being made are true or are not true, and, if they are true, that prompt action is taken in order to remedy the condition thereby presented.
My whole argument was based on the fact that when references have been made to the Combines Investigation Act and the Wartime Prices and Trade Board Act the government was accused of leaving these problems to bureaucrats. I wished it understood that the matter was now being left to the people's representatives in the House of Commons by way of fact finding so as to make immediate action possible without obstacles being presented by difficulties in procedure under the Combines Investigation Act or the other act.
I think it is clear, if hon. gentlemen opposite agree with a decision given by a previous Speaker to the effect that an amendment is out of order if it raises a new question not contemplated in the notice of that motion, then, Mr. Speaker, you will have to decide what was contemplated in the motion. If Your Honour decides that a new question is raised by the amendment that was not contemplated by the wording of the motion itself or by what specifically was said by the government in introducing the motion as to what was thereby contemplated, the amendment, I submit, should be ruled out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I submit with all deference that if there is doubt as to what was involved in the wording of the original motion, in other words as to what was contemplated, Your Honour must make your decision on the basis of the written word. I submit that the government has no right to contend that its statement adds to or detracts from the words of the original motion, and that Your Honour must make your decision on the basis of the motion and the amendments which are now before you.
It seems to me that this boils down to a matter of interpretation. In other words, Your Honour has to decide whether the subject matter of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and of the amendment which I moved this afternoon introduces new material. Is the material

germane to the original motion, or is it foreign to it? Opinions expressed on the two sides of the house differ on that point. All of us on this side seem to agree that both amendments are germane to the question.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, and with this I conclude, that if there is a doubt in your mind you should turn to May's Parliamentary Practice, 13th edition, where at page 278 I read these words:
The forms of the house can ultimately assist neither party: but, so far as they offer any intermediate advantage, the minority have the greatest protection in forms.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, according to May, if there is a clear doubt the benefit of the doubt should go to the minority because the only advantage they have otherwise is that of debate. It seems quite clear, from the discussion which has taken place thus far, that it is a matter of doubt whether the subject matter of the amendment and the subamendment introduces new material, and I strongly urge Your Honour to make your decision on the basis of the text of the amendments and not on the basis of what the Prime Minister has said the government contemplated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) had just concluded his remarks on this motion. I listened very carefully to what he said. Unfortunately, like all members of his socialist party, he feels that in each speech he must attack free enterprise. He ridiculed the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) on behalf of freedom and free enterprise, and referred to free enterprise as a system of tyranny and as the acts of some few in exploiting the community, and as usual he made his plea for state control and absolute regimentation. These socialist C.C.F.-ers always forget that Canada has reached the position she occupies today, not under C.C.F. policies, but under free enterprise and private initiative.
I would also remind the hon. member for Vancouver East and other members of the socialist party that all their members were elected to this free parliament under our system of democratic government. How many members do they think they would ever elect

Prices Committee
to any parliament if we followed the system of Soviet Russia? The socialists would clearly love to regiment and control the whole economic life of this nation. In short, they seek to enslave the Canadian population with their fantastic Karl Marx theories. Their system of complete regimentation would take away from the youth of our country all initiative and ambition. No one needs to tell me that the youth of Canada have not great opportunities under free enterprise in this country. What opportunity would they have under a government which believed in practising complete state regimentation? Those of us who served in the army and came under its discipline would think our army days were a de luxe vacation compared with life under a socialist program of complete state regimentation. I submit that the youth of Canada have the opportunity of education and advancement by their own merit. How can you ever replace this advantage by having some half-baked government theorist tell the youth of Canada what occupation or profession they are to follow, or what work is to be allotted to them?
I know in my own family I have watched my four children approach the age when the time came to choose for themselves the profession or the occupation they intended to follow. When that time came, the choice was not made by their mother; the choice was not made by myself; the choice was not made by any official of any of the various schools they attended; the choice was not made by any socialist government official; it was made by each individual for himself or herself. To me that is one of the greatest rights we have in Canada. One of the greatest rights is that the youth of Canada shall have the opportunity of deciding and choosing for himself or herself what occupation or profession he or she intends to follow in this country. It seems to me that the ambitions and the desires that are inbred in all the youth of Canada can be fulfilled only by their remaining free and uncontrolled by any socialist state.
I often wonder, Mr. Speaker, as you sit in this house day after day and are forced to listen, as you are, to the socialist doctrines expounded by the C.C.F., how you must shudder when you contemplate this Canada of ours ever being under the heel of a socialist C.C.F. party.
Coming to the motion before the house, may I say that if there has been any doubt in the mind of any hon. member as to the utter farce of the setting up of this committee it has all been dispelled by the proceedings which took place in this chamber tonight from eight o'clock until a quarter to nine. It has
been clearly demonstrated that the government as usual sets out to whitewash and to hide the real facts.
You may read the motion as carefully as you wish or in any legal way, or add to it or detract from it, but the fact remains that the simple words of paragraph (a) cover the whole thing, "(a) the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living." I ask you, Mr. Speaker, in your capacity as a learned counsel of the law, how can you ever approach any case without having all the facts before you? A court of law insists that all the facts be presented to it before any decision can be made. If this committee is set up along the lines suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) -by that I mean that the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and the subamendment thereto are defeated- then I for one am firmly convinced that this committee will simply result in a fishing expedition, and at the end of a long, long course it will finish up with no fish and will not have a little aside enjoyment that usually goes with fishing expeditions.
Despite the memorandum read by the Prime Minister as reported at page 750 of Hansard, which is a memorandum submitted to him by the Clerk of the House, I fear that when this committee is set up hon. members in the future will be denied the right to speak on any of the matters mentioned in the terms of reference of this committee; because I do not need to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that on various other occasions when committees have been set up, time and time again an appeal has been made to Your Honour and Your Honour has ruled out of order attempts that are made to discuss certain matters on the ground that they were before a committee of the house.
I would emphasize the remarks made by my leader yesterday when he so ably pointed out that at the present time the wartime prices and trade board has all the powers, all the authority, all the staff and all the machinery necessary to investigate the very subject matter that it is to be sent to this committee.
Personally I have never had any use for the wartime prices and trade board. I have often described it as an octopus and said in this house that it was an octopus strangling business in this country, but perhaps now it could be put to some use. If there has been profiteering there is provision for the prosecution of profiteers. I have noticed over the years that the wartime prices and trade board were always very eager to prosecute. Now they have a glorious opportunity, but I would
Prices Committee

suggest that they take advantage of it and get at the facts, and, if it is necessary to prosecute, let them prosecute.
During the war years and after, I often heard members of the Liberal party in this house compare the cost of living after the first great war with the cost of living during and after the war just concluded. These Liberal members have always placed the blame on the Tory government which was in power during the first great war. How they assured us time and time again that there would not be such repetition at the end of the war just ended; that under the wise planning of the Prime Minister and his advisers everything was planned and everything would be taken care of. Yet today we find in Canada that prices are practically as high as they were after the end of the first great war. Some hon. members may disagree with that, but if they do I would point out first that they have forgotten to mention the income tax. Those of us who are old enough to remember the income tax after the first great war know that the amount of income tax which the ordinary individual paid was a mere trifle compared with the tax today.
The income tax today imposes a most crushing burden on the small wage earner, especially the white-collar class, the married man with a small family and the unmarried woman who works in an office, factory or store. The cost of living of these people, the cost of their clothes and everything else has practically doubled. Regardless of this, the income tax is the first item that has to be paid, irrespective of whether or not the individual has sufficient money left to provide a decent standard of living for himself and his dependents.
Take the case of the newly established veteran who is trying to re-establish himself in civilian life with his re-establishment credits, and who is trying to make up in some way for what he lost during the years that he served in the armed forces of Canada. He finds that all the cream is skimmed off in taxes and income tax. Not only has he this excessive income tax to pay, but he is saddled with numerous other taxes.
I should like to refer to page 775 of Hansard of yesterday when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), in a manner which he does not often use, referred to certain remarks made by the leader of the opposition in an attempt to answer the leader of the opposition in his reference to certain hidden taxes. He referred only to the taxes on spirits and tobacco. There is no doubt that the Secretary of State for External Affairs

knew very well that the leader of the opposition was not referring to the taxes on spirits and tobacco.
While the minister spoke on cigarettes and tobacco, I would say to him that he might well consider the possibility of reducing the tax on tobacco. He says that we can do without them. Certainly we can do without them. We can also do without tea and coffee, ice-cream, shoes, boots; we could go bare-headed; we could wear no gloves and other things as we saw fit; but, after all, these are things that enter into our way of life.
If the minister had wished to be fair, he might also have referred to the twenty-five per cent tax on luxury goods, or on what I say are wrongly called luxury goods, Which applies to such things as leather products, travelling bags, watches, clocks, pens, glassware, silver plate, electrical goods and many other articles. I should like to ask the minister if he considers that a fair tax or one that might be abolished. What does the minister think of the position of the veteran who is setting up a home or of the young couple who are starting their first home and are met with this heavy tax which is called a luxury tax, but which is a tax imposed on the necessities of life?
The minister might well have mentioned the eight per cent sales tax which is imposed on practically everything that we buy. I wonder if the minister ever considered whether some reduction in the sales tax and in this so-called luxury tax might have something to do with reducing the cost of living? And the same thing applies to the taxes imposed last November by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Does the minister think the restrictions on the importation of green vegetables helped to lower the cost of living when, in fact, those restrictions put the price of Canadian vegetables up to an unheard of level at a time when it was impossible for the Canadian producer to produce vegetables? Does the minister consider it is necessary or wise to add another heavy tax on motorcars produced and manufactured in this country? Perhaps he wants us to return to the horse-and-buggy days. There are many other taxes which I might mention to the minister, but I would point out again that he confined his remarks to taxes on liquor and tobacco.
The Prime Minister, in his remarks on moving this resolution, stated that high prices prevailed not only in Canada but in other countries. How different that statement was

Prices Committee
from many other statements made by followers of the Prime Minister in this house. For years I have heard talk about the depression days of 1930 to 1935, and the heaping of the blame for that on the Bennett government. But today when we find1 a somewhat similar condition existing, the government is attempting at this late date to load its responsibility on the shoulders of a committee. Some of us can remember what the government promised to the veterans in the way of homes. Yet we have only to read1 the press to learn of the sorry mess in which the veterans find themselves in the Windsor area with regard to the homes they bought there. In the last session we were told by the former minister of veterans affairs that it would cost the taxpayers of this country somewhere between $500,000 and $750,000 to make the necessary repairs to new veterans' homes, which repairs should have been made in full by the contractors.
In the matter of pensions we find that there has been no increase for well over twenty years. At this late day, after months and years of prodding, the government have announced that the basic rate will be increased by the magnificent amount of ten per cent. All I would say, Mr. Speaker, is that I cannot understand1 how any veteran member of this House of Commons could rise in his place and praise this small increase in the basic pension rate, having in mind the terrific increase in the cost of living. I submit that if the Prime Minister is really sincere in his attempt to find out the true facts in connection with the recent increase in the cost of living, he and his followers will accept the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition:	because there can be little
exception taken to the various amendments set out in paragraphs (d), '(e), (f) and (g) or to the addition of paragraph 2. But I fear that it has already been indicated that the Prime Minister is not willing to accept the amendment. If the amendment is defeated I can only repeat that when the committee is set up it will turn out to be another whitewash committee, on a useless fishing trip.

My suggestion is that my hon. friend is not only trying to ride two horses, but trying to ride them in opposite directions-with the only physical and political result possible.
In a brief review of the situation I think it can be truthfully said that, during the war years, some of the controls advocated by some of the hon. members of this house were set up. They were set in motion by this government. Right across the board we had controls on industry and agriculture. We had controls, of course, on wages. I know something about the difficulties and complexities of the administration of those controls. I know something, as do my hon. friends, of the criticism that was levelled at Mr. Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board; and I of course know something of the criticisms that were levelled at myself as chairman of the national war labour board. It is a strange thing that today we see members of all parties opposite wanting some of the controls established on one phase of the economy and no controls on the other. The contribution made by controls to the well-being of the Canadian people during that war period was the equal at least of that made in any other country. That was generally recognized with the conclusion of the war. Let me say that I appreciate, as I think do all hon. members in this house, that over and above the law of the land there is a more powerful motivating force, and that is a desire for the survival of the way of life which, in my judgment, was the real driving spirit of those controls. I think that was

Prices Committee

generally conceded at the time by all elements in Canada, whether or not they have changed their minds since. My hon. friends opposite advocated the abolition of all controls; I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) took that position.

there was not the frank admission that you cannot get something for nothing, that if you have a subsidy, by the very nature of the thing it is an indirect tax. Now the official opposition argue for lower prices, some controls, and lower taxes. In my judgment, in this debate they present a good example of confused finance and basic economics. Let me say to the hon. member for Stanstead that, whether we like it or not, old age pensions, children's allowances, workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance, veterans' allowances and all these great social forces in the life of this or any other nation by the very nature of things are a charge on the living standards of the people.
I want to say further that I have advocated these great social policies all my life. I believe in them because I believe it is absolutely necessary, if a nation is to prevent disorder and revolution, that it should continually redistribute its wealth. In our way of life a government must exist to protect the weak against the strong; but I think it should be clearly understood, in all these measures of taxation, that by the very nature of things they are the redistribution of the wealth of a nation.
I am wholly in support of the establishment of this committee because I think the public of Canada generally want it. It is necessary for several reasons. One is to determine where and in what commodities there have been exorbitant price rises beyond all necessity except a desire to cash in at the expense

Prices Committee
of our citizens. The main responsibility of this parliament is to protect the people we represent. That has always been the policy of the Liberal party, and that is what we are setting out to do through this committee.
I should like to point out that there is also another very good reason for the pending inquiry. Throughout Canada, thanks to the calculated suggestions of opponents of our way of life, the feeling has grown that profiteers are rampant in the country. I think that is very unfair to our businessmen.

The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is a classic example of that very simple fact. Let me say, in passing, that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is, in my opinion, the most advanced and most sensible form of industrial relations machinery ever devised by any government. Mr. Speaker, I feel a little out of place taking part in the debate at this time because so many of the government big guns have been brought into action. W hen we came here on December 5 we were given to understand that we were to open an emergency session of parliament, but before we left we were given to understand that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) wanted to call a caucus and we were thus given a chance to have a trip
Prices Committee

to Ottawa. After listening to this debate on the setting up of a committee to investigate the high cost of living, a debate which has lasted almost two days, one begins to wonder whether the Prime Minister is not using this occasion to have the potential leaders of the Liberal party strut their stuff before the house and the country.
I can remember 'back in 1934 just before I came to the house the Stevens inquiry was held, during which a lot of useful information was brought out. However, in the 1935 election the present government was victorious at the polls and Mr. Stevens' party lost out, although he got one seat. The present government does not seem to have taken very much advantage of the information which was brought out by that royal commission.
A little later, in 1937 and 1938, the agriculture committee of the House of Commons investigated the prices of farm implements. Before that committee turned in its report, the machine companies made two increases in the prices of implements. Yesterday, February 2, the Prime Minister introduced a resolution to set up a committee to investigate the high cost of living. In today's Ottawa Citizen and Ottawa Journal there is a small article tucked away in the corner under a Montreal date line of February 2, which reads:
A railway spokesman said tonight that effective today meals on railway dining cars in Canada will be subject to a ten per cent increase.
I believe that the government railroad is included in that announcement. The subamendment, which I believe will be dealt with first, reads:
And in particular to examine and report upon:
(e) measures to stem the rising cost of living, such as the restoration of price controls and subsidies, the examination of these matters to be the committee's first order of business and a report thereon 'to be presented to this house not later than three weeks from the day of the committee's first meeting.
I do not see very much the matter with that. Judging from the speed at which we are moving tonight, three weeks will not be sufficient to enable the committee to bring in that portion of its report. Starting at eight o'clock this evening, a discussion lasting forty-five minutes took place as to whether the amendment and the subamendment were in order. That was not precipitated by any opposition member; it was precipitated by one of the government's parliamentary assistants, and we seem to be still in the dark as far as that matter is concerned.
I shall not be surprised if the amendments are ruled out of order or in order. At the

present time we have five books of rules. Three were made up by the present Clerk of the House, and we have Bourinot's rules and May's rules. If a section cannot be found in one of those books to suit the occasion, it can be found in another. The second part of the subamendment reads:
And in particular to examine and report upon:
(f)	measures to control the prices of commodities entering into the farmers' costs of production in view of the fact that controls are maintained on the prices of farm products.
It seems strange that every time controls are to be exercised, agriculture is the first industry to bear the brunt. Listening to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon and looking back to December 19 when he made another speech, those who do not know any better might feel that everything on the farm was fine and rosy. Many people here are perhaps ready to believe that everything the minister tells them is just as he tells it. However, many of us who have had experience in farming know that the pictures are not all just as they are painted.
Just a few days after that memorable stock growers' meeting in Lethbridge which the minister attended, I heard some delegates to that meeting discuss the meeting in Edmonton as well as the minister. They gave me the same opinion as I have had of him at different times. Somebody says, "Tell us what he is." I am going to do that right away. This is not my opinion; it is the opinion of some of the delegates to that stock growers' convention. They said, "The little devil is hard to catch up with, but when you do catch him he is so slippery you cannot hold on to him." Those are not my words. I must admit, as I have on other occasions, that the minister is entitled to credit for doing a lot of fighting on behalf of the farmers of Canada, and I am not limiting that to the farmers of the prairie provinces. I know that while the minister is a small man, fighting practically alone, though possibly he has one or two helpers, there are many other bigger and heavier men whom he has to fight against and he cannot hope to win the battle every time, but I hope that he will continue to fight for the farmers as well as he has done in the past.
Many people today feel that the farmers are living in a land of milk and honey. I admit frankly that the farmers are in a better financial position today than they have been in for quite a while, but let us take a look back over some of the other years. Let us look back to the period from 1930 to 1940.

Prices Committee
At that time we were living in a depression period brought about by men who are still exercising some of their wickedness today and who have been given the power by legislation passed here from time to time to continue that wickedness and persecute our Canadian people.
Today people are complaining about the price of roast beef, roast lamb, roast pork, butter, eggs and many other things; but if we go back to the depression period from 1930 to 1940, and particularly 1935, I can well remember selling the best milch cows and the best steers for ten and twelve dollars a head. People forget those times. I remember selling the best wheat that could be grown in the world for 19Y>
cents a bushel, and it cost us fourteen cents a bushel to thresh it. Again I remember seeing people sell the best oats that could be grown in Canada at eight cents a bushel, the best grade A eggs at three cents a dozen, butter at eight cents a pound, and live hogs at 214 cents a pound. So, when people are discussing the high cost of living today, I would ask them to look back to those days and ask them whether any assistance was given to the farmers at that time, by government or private individuals, to help them through that period of difficulty.
It must not be forgotten that during the early years of the war we were still receiving, not because we wanted to, depression prices for our agricultural products. We were told that we must be patriotic and do our bit to feed our own people and the people overseas, and the farmers of Canada certainly did a worthwhile job. They produced enough food for everybody in Canada and produced millions and millions of dollars worth of food to send overseas.
Then, in return for these sacrifices we were told that when the war was over we would get the advantages of higher prices to compensate for the low prices we had been accepting up to that time. The minister has told us that on different occasions, just as he did again today. He told us of the legislation that was passed, providing for a $200 million fund to stabilize prices. But, as I have often stated before, the basis on which those prices are established is false and should be rectified before any further prices are set. The prices are, I understand, based on prices existing betwen 1926 and 1929; but at that time the farmers of Canada, representing approximately one-third of our total population, received only 16-6 per cent of the national income. We remember that during the years 1930 to 1940 the farmers of Canada received only 9-4 per cent of the national income, and in 1932, 5 per cent, which represented $198 per farm all across the country.
Again we were told that we would have stabilization when the war was over. We have a certain degree of stabilization until our contracts with Britain expire, but after that time there is no guarantee of stabilization for the agricultural industry and no legislation providing for that. In Canada not many months ago we were wondering whether our wheat agreement with Britain would still hold good. Since then, certain agreements have been completed with Britain and it looks as though we shall have a fair price for a short time at least.
Again I would remind the house of the sacrifices that have been borne by our Canadian farmers. I am doing that at this time because people feel that the farmers are living in a land of milk and honey. I would ask the consumers of Canada to remember that during the war we subsidized the people who eat bread, and you all remember the howl which went up on August 1 last when a little increase in the price of wheat for making into flour became effective. In addition we subsidized the brewers and distillers of Canada, so that people could' buy drinks cheaper and the government get still more taxes from that source.
Again do not forget that we subsidized the markets of the world, commencing September, 1943, when the ceiling price of $1.55 was established on all our export wheat, regardless of the fact that wheat in the United States and other countries was selling at a much higher price. The farmers were compelled by government policy to stand the whole cost of this subsidy. Under the British wheat agreement, do not forget again that the farmers of Canada are subsidizing the people of Britain on the purchase of 600,000,000 bushels of wheat. May I ask the government-the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is now in his seat and I ask him-why the farmers Qf Canada have been compelled to pay all during these years the whole cost of that subsidy. Perhaps before the end of this debate or the end of the session, when he has had time to consider the matter, he will tell us why.
Again we have provided cheap coarse grains, so that the people of Canada could produce and get more foodstuffs. That cost was borne entirely by the farmers of the prairie provinces.
As I have asked on several occasions before, I ask again tonight that provision be made to transfer from the general revenue fund of this country to the wheat board fund an amount representing the difference between what was received by our farmers and the world market price of wheat, so that it can be distributed to its proper owners, the farmers who grew and delivered the grain.

Prices Committee

Now that the cost of living is high, we find that the farmers are again being attacked. But we have not heard very much about-placing ceilings on the cost of farm tractors and other farm machinery and other items entering into farm- production costs. But we see ceilings placed on butter, and on- meat in the very near future, and we do not know where all this is going to stop.
May I suggest to the government that in order to bring down the cost of living they remove many of the hidden taxes, reduce the income tax levy, increase the exemption before any taxes are levied and remove all the obstacles that stand in the way of increased production; because, as has been said on many occasions in this house, the best way to bring down the cost of living is to increase our production to the point where consumers will have sufficient goods to meet their demands.
Another way in which it can be done is to increase the amount of the family allowance. We know that can be done. Increase the old age pension; increase the war veterans allowance; increase the war pensions; increase the allowance to veteran students. I am not going to stop there. I say we should increase the income of all those people in any occupation whatever who have not sufficient to provide themselves and their families with a decent standard of living. This country can provide it. We have provided over $20 billion to fight a war planned by man, and we have gone into debt to a very great extent for that amount of money and not necessarily so. Let us see if we cannot, for the benefit of our Canadian people, increase the standard of living of our people and do something constructive rather than destructive.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not as one just wishing to express a-formal opposition to this resolution as sponsored by the government, but .as one who considers it his duty to express the opinion of the great majority of the people he has the honour to represent, an opinion which has been expressed in no uncertain terms.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that since December 3 last I have received from various organizations and individuals living within the constituency which I have the honour to represent, just something over fourteen hundred communications dealing with the cost of living and urging price control, subsidies and necessary adjustments.
In view of the fact that the government has recognized the present rise in the cost of living it is inconceivable to me that the people of this country have to wait, and in some cases continue to suffer, while this matter is dealt

with by a parliamentary committee which is supposed to get the basic facts which are already known to everyone in this house.
The basic fact is simply this, that the rapidly rising prices in recent months have increased the cost of living so that many people in this country do not enjoy a satisfactory standard of living. In my opinion, that is the basic fact, and we all know that. Today I received a copy of a paper published in my constituency, the Nelson Daily News. The headline says: "Kootenay output for 1947, 150 millions". That represents the output of one of the richest districts in Canada, an output composed of minerals, forestry products and the products of the farm. If it were redistributed that total output would mean an income of something over $2,500 to every person residing within that district. At the same time I have received something over fourteen hundred communications from people expressing their opinions regarding the cost of living, how they are affected by the cost of living and urging price control and subsidies. Does one require any more evidence of the need for some further redistribution of wealth through price control and subsidies?
During the Christmas recess I took the opportunity to visit a good many of my constituents. I .am not going to deal with a lot of figures this evening; in fact I am going to be quite brief, but I like to find out what the people are thinking. I visited the homes of industrial workers in the cities of Trail, Rossland and Nelson, and questioned the wives of these men concerning the cost of living and so on. There I found a definite concern with the difficulties they are having in making their pay cheques meet the cost of living. That was not discontent stirred up by a so-called agitator. That was the honest concern of many of what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) referred to this evening as good solid Canadian citizens.
I visited a number of the farmers. I found the livestock producers, the pork and beef producers-there is some beef produced in my riding-very much concerned about the increased cost of feed, but even more concerned about the uncertainty of the future. I find the same condition existing in the poultry industry. We have quite a large and growing poultry industry in my constituency. I visited a number of poultry farms and found that in many cases the poultrymen did not know what to do for the coming year. They had placed orders a month or so previously for a large number of baby chicks which have to arrive early in the spring. Because of the increased cost of food, and more particularly because of the uncertainty as to the future, many of them were cancelling their chick orders.

Prices Committee
I visited the homes of veterans, particularly those on disability pension and war veterans' allowance. Some of these people are suffering severely. I visited the home of one man who received a war veterans' allowance. He lives in a little log home and pays no rent. I asked him how he was managing to get along on his $30 a month. He said, "Well, I could just get by till recently; now, during the last six months, I find it impossible, owing to the increased cost of living, to make ends meet". I found the same condition amongst those receiving widows' allowance; I found the very same condition in the case of those receiving old age pensions and also with a small number of people who have to live on small fixed incomes from small investments and annuities.
In addition to the insecurity created by conditions among these groups of people, I found numbers of young people, veterans and others, who are desiring to build and furnish homes, very much concerned about the future and hesitating to take any action in that direction because of the uncertainty as to the price structure in the months ahead. The same thing applies to the development of farms. I found a number of people who have purchased raw land, who are delaying the construction of buildings, delaying investment in and development of the land because they are not certain of the future with respect to prices. I found generally a sense of insecurity, a sense of instability regarding the future. That is why, not only in my constituency but all across Canada, we find this very strong and unified demand for price control and subsidies on certain essential articles.
Now, Mr. Speaker, no one has disputed that the government has all the legislation necessary to effect controls. That legislation is on the statute books. Government speakers in this debate have admitted they have the power to do that. According to a press report of the Ottawa Evening Journal of January 31, 1946, even officials of the government have threatened that the government will take action if prices are increased unnecessarily. I want to quote this from the Ottawa Evening Journal of January 31, 1946:
If costs climb out of line with the general fabric of the price structure both Mr. Ilsley and prices board chairman Donald Gordon promised that the ceilings again would be imposed.
In a letter to hundreds of Canadian manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, Mr. Gordon emphasized that the ceilings were being suspended not cancelled.
Mr. Ilsley added the admonition that any abuse of this new price freedom would result in reimposition of the ceilings.
Regardless of the fact that a minister of the crown and government officials have threatened 5849-53J
the imposition of price ceilings, we find government speakers and leading members of the government now speaking in the opposite direction so far as general policy is concerned. No one disputes the financial capacity of this country to pay whatever subsidies may be necessary to keep prices down. I think that is a fact, particularly in view of the information we have of a possible large surplus this fiscal year. No one disputes the demand of the Canadian people for the reimposition of certain controls and subsidies. I think public opinion is very well expressed in that direction, and we find it coming from many different groups in the community.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, no one disputes the success of price controls and subsidies during the war, or objects to giving the government credit for the good work done at that time. In my opinion, and without doubt in- the opinion of the majority of the Canadian people at this time, there is only one satisfactory method of restoring stability to our price structure, a stability which is necessary to restore a feeling of security and confidence in our people. That is, first, to restore price controls on all basic necessities; second, to restore subsidies on essential foods and also on coarse grains, and, third, to restore the 100 per cent excess profits tax.
In introducing this motion, I think the Prime Minister pointed out that one of the purposes of the committee was to shed light on certain questions. In that connection I wish to say that in the past we have had . a good many investigations which were supposed to shed light on certain questions and bring about certain results. I remember some years ago an investigation into the control of the sale of fruit on the prairies by certain, interests; it was a lengthy investigation to-shed some light on the question. I think those interests were fined a mere pittance, so. far as their large organization was concerned, and then on they go as usual. We have had other investigations with similar results. In my opinion and, I think, in the opinion of a good many other people in this country, persons of this type will understand only one thing, and that is the will of the people as expressed in law through parliament, giving effect to price controls.
Why does the government propose a committee of this type rather than accept the undeniably expressed will of the Canadian people through many channels? It does so, I think because it recognizes the state of public opinion and the necessity of doing something; but that something must be as little as possible. I am not blaming the members of the

speechtext:
I should like to give a
ruling on the amendment which is before the house. The Prime Minister moved that a select committee be appointed to examine
(a)	the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living; (b) prices which have been raised above levels justified by increased costs; and
(c)	rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating and withholding from sale of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of business.
The leader of the opposition moved in amendment that the committee be also empowered to examine "the effect of present government policies in lessening Canadian agricultural production."
I cannot overlook the fact that this is too important a question to be moved as corollary to the appointment of such a committee as the one now being proposed. It is against all parliamentary usage to refer questions of policy to fact-finding committees. I find that the great Speaker Denison decided in 1877-see decisions of Speaker Denison, published by Edwin Gordon Blackmore, page 210-and his decision still holds good, that:
It is not competent, without notice, to add a distinct question to a motion, or to combine in one two distinct propositions.
Of course I must add that, when an amendment is irregular in one particular, the whole of it is not admissible and must be ruled out of order.
This is sound practice and, for that reason, I declare the amendment out of order. It follows that the subamendment cannot be moved. I must add, however, for the information of the house, that the amendment to the amendment will be barred for the same reason.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with you absolutely. The reason I am interjecting some remarks into this debate is a good one. If we approve the setting up of this committee the government will have denied to the opposition and to all others in this house who think otherwise the right to rise in their places and criticize what we believe is the real reason for prices having fluctuated and the cost of living having reached heights unprecedented in the history of Canada.
This afternoon we were privileged to hear a dissertation from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). He dwelt at considerable length upon how increased costs of production affected the Canadian producer. No one can find fault with his eloquence or oratory; but I think we should come down from the heights of oratory and deal with one cold fact, namely, that one of the things which has increased the post of living in this country is the -tremendous cost of government. If you take -the per capita tax at -the present time and compare it with what it was a few years ago you will find that, the increase in the cost of living is still below the increase in the cost of government of this country.
May I reply directly to the Minister of Agriculture? I represent a rural constituency, two-thirds of my constituents being rural and about one-third being urban dwellers. I think they know the answer now, certainly the far-mere do. When the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin)

addressed a public meeting a short time ago he indicated that the government had a solution of their problems which would be given out in the matter of two or three days, and then the Minister of Agriculture stated he was prepared to offer something to sustain agriculture in its economic relation to the rest of the Dominion of Canada. However, the fact remains that the only thing the government is offering to us is a committee to investigate those who are profiteering.
We cannot be unmindful of the fact that during the last session of the house the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) budgeted for subsidies. Those subsidies are not being paid. When those subsidies were discontinued the farmers of Canada did not know where to turn.
I want to give the house the most realistic picture I could possibly bring before it. On the livestock market in the city of Toronto, at the union stockyards, the farmers were offering for sale their brood sows. Those sows were having little pigs right there on the market, and they were being devoured by the other pigs. I know whereof I speak. I agree with my hon. friend the member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) that the time is not far distant when those who are responsible for this state of confusion in the over-all economy of Canada will be crying out for bacon not only to fill our British contracts but to satisfy the demands of the home market.
The subsidy on feed grain was discontinued. It is true that a promise was made at that time; but no one knew the extent of that promise, and the farmers of Canada were left in a vacuum and, lacking any sense of direction, marketed their breeding stock. The farmers of Canada were promised something they knew not what. Then the British contracts were negotiated, and that was followed by the most disastrous event that one could contemplate. Breeding stock was sold on the market, and it will take some time to repair that loss and the disruption that it caused in our agricultural production program. I have always taken the view that you should not let go of one thing until you have something else to take its place. I say to the government that after it had collected from the Canadian taxpayer to maintain subsidies, those subsidies should have been maintained until there was something else to take their place, and the people of Canada, particularly the farmers, should have been told what the government was seeking to do. But our farmers are resourceful. They proved that constantly during the war, and they are prepared to put their shoulder to the wheel at the present time. But everyone wants to know in what direction we are going.

Prices Committee

speechtext: Indeed it was a good speech and I enjoyed listening to him. One might think sometimes that this country was run by supermen, but after analysing the minister's speech 1 was reminded of those who try to sell you something when the substance is really not there. He overlooked one basic fact, and that was the multiplication of costs which have been built up by this government in relation to our individual problems. There is the parity of exchange, the gold situation, bureaucracy. I know he does not like that word and I do not like it either, but I know that we are governed today by influences and sources outside this house. The government has become so imbued with its wartime mentality and the right to do almost as it pleases, passing 90,000 orders in council, that it no longer considers that the voice of parliament counts for anything. If you want to get the greatest possible benefits of the productive capacity of this nation there is a clear and open road to that end, and that is to apply sound business judgment in the Department of Finance, and not to over-budget. The budget of the Minister of Finance indicated a lack of faith in Canada. The government have indeed become the first profiteers in Canada. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), interrupting a speaker in this debate the other night, said that he believed the profiteers were our greatest menace. I say to him that if he knows of any profiteers in Canada he should be the first witness to come before this committee, because we want to know right now who are the profiteers.

It may bring in certain reports to the house, but it is not required to do so by the terms of reference. It is not privileged to make recommendations. The net results is that we shall be no further ahead three or four months from now or even when prorogation takes place.
It is all very well for the Minister of Agriculture to talk about the prosperity of Canada; but ask the people who have the exchange in their pockets what it is costing them to live today compared with just a few weeks ago when the Prime Minister made his stirring address from overseas with respect to the Geneva trade agreements which we all thought was a move in the right direction to bring about greater world-wide trade, only to be followed by the address of the Minister of Finance which nullified the whole thing.
If the ministry are honestly seeking reasons for the increased cost of living today let them look in their own offices; let them look at their own employees and they will see the over-all cost of government and the tremendous taxation levied upon the Canadian people in relation to that which existed a few years ago. You want greater prosperity; you want greater production. Then I ask the government to give consideration to a tremendous cut in taxation, to stir up the enthusiasm, the enterprise and the ambition of the Canadian people, and you will not long have to worry about the costs of living in the Dominion of Canada, this land of great ' promise, this land of plenty if we only had the proper leadership to show us the way.
